due to various structural and functional changes. This is what is referred to as progressive overload.  However, it 
is inappropriate to apply this principle literally, since research has revealed that optimal progress is made if the  
increased loading phases are alternated periodically with decreased loading phases  (see Ch 6). Continual

stagnation or injury. It is vital to remember that tissue repair and growth occur predominantly during the 
restoration and transition periods between training sessions and not during the heavy loading phases.

produce the same, predetermined maximal level of resistance. It has been hypothesised that they cause the body 
to over-adapt, or supercompensate , to a somewhat higher level, in physiological anticipation of repeated exposure 
to the same stressor (Fig 1.39).

# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (via Siff) argues "adaptive reconstruction" is a more
accurate term than "supercompensation" for the body's response to training load, for two
specific reasons stated in the text: (1) enhanced performance is not simply the result of
increased stores of bioenergetic substances (the energy-overshoot picture supercompensation
implies), but also of structural changes in muscle and connective tissue and enhanced
efficiency of bioenergetic and neuromuscular processing; (2) no supercompensation has been
observed for any bioenergetic substance except glycogen — other biochemicals deplete under
strenuous exercise but do not overshoot their baseline afterward, and each returns to
baseline on its own timeline, making the timing of a "supercompensation window" for
non-glycogen substances indeterminate. Russian sources use "Current Adaptation Reserves"
(CAR) for the readily-available (superficial) and emergency (deep) energy sources drawn on
during Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome resistance phase. (PDF pp. 94-96, printed pp.
83-85.)

**Why it works** — If supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant substance
or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training stimulus
to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the empirical finding that this overshoot
pattern is essentially unique to glycogen undercuts that precision and supports treating
"the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general heuristic, not a substance-by-
substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
include; use both together rather than duplicating either.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
on periodization design.

**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
by the same evidence.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

**Why it works** — The deficit is attributed to a neural, not mechanical, limitation:
reduced activation of the prime movers during simultaneous bilateral effort, which
training the specific bilateral pattern appears to reduce over time — another instance of
narrow, mode-specific neuromuscular adaptation.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back
squat, bench, clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise
variants, match the training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports
with genuinely unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and
change-of-direction actions), this text's finding argues for meaningful unilateral training
exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts, since bilateral-only training may under-develop
the single-limb activation football and track actions require. This football-specific
application is this entry's own extension, not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts
altogether; compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are
appropriate where the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting
actions). Verkhoshansky gives no specific deficit magnitude for team-sport athletes in
this section (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28); **Inference:** the deficit's size and
trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, which is this entry's own caution.

**Example** — **Inference:** A sprinter's single-leg force production during ground contact is not fully
predicted by their bilateral back squat strength alone; programming that includes
single-leg strength work targets the bilateral deficit gap directly relevant to sprint and
change-of-direction performance.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]].

# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First

**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)

**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
an injury mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research (ACL specifically), not a live-tissue,
in-vivo human athlete dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase,
the fourfold rate figure) as applicable outside the original ACL loading-rate study cited.
This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
clinical exam in determining actual injury location.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

Strenuous exercise lasting between approximately 6-30 seconds activates oxygen-independent glycolysis 
maximally, but appropriate rest intervals will prevent a serious increase in blood lactate. This is the rationale 
behind the value of interval and fartlek (repeated jog-sprint) running, and interval circuit training with weights or 
machines. In the gymnasium setting, development of endurance in specific muscle groups is facilitated by ICT 
(interval circuit training), which permits the use of fairly heavy loads, alternating with rest phases of 30-60 
seconds between stations. The sub-maximal nature of most ICT, however, does not enhance strength and power 
sufficiently to meet the specific needs of strength and speed sports, except possibly during the early off-season.
Oxygen-independent glycolysis reaches its peak after about 30-40 seconds, and after 90-120 seconds its 
contribution becomes minimal, being replaced by oxygen-dependent glycolysis  (Fig 1.37). This process becomes 
the dominant energy-producer for all long duration, low intensity activities such as distance running and cycling. 
If the exercise intensity is kept below the blood lactate tumpoint, the lactate and protons will be removed at the 
same rate as their production so that prolonged muscle activity becomes possible.

which traditionally have been used to offer a rough guide to anyone who devises sport specific training routines to

# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit

**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine
manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops
cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity
loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength
and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity
endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously
compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start
behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies
of distance runners' gastrocnemius after a marathon show necrosis and inflammation
detectable at least 7 days later, an abnormality not seen in comparable biopsies from
weightlifters, sprinters, or rowers after strenuous sessions. (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59.)

**Why it works** — Continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work trains the aerobic/oxidative
system and biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch characteristics, which is a different
and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the high-force, high-velocity, largely
fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's rest intervals let each work bout
stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific zone instead of drifting toward
an endurance stimulus.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming
that needs to develop both conditioning and strength: the text's recommendation is to
prescribe cardiovascular training separately, in limited amounts, early in the off-season,
with higher-intensity resistance training emphasized later, and to use interval-style
(work/rest) circuits rather than continuous circuits when the goal includes
strength-endurance. **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own
conditioning priority stack for football (alactic and aerobic capacity/power first, with
glycolytic conditioning absorbed incidentally rather than programmed as a primary target;
`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34,
39`), though the baseline material does not itself cite this fibre-type mechanism.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is evidence against combining continuous,
prolonged low-intensity work with concurrent strength training in the same block, not an
argument against all conditioning; short, high-intensity interval conditioning is treated
as more compatible with strength/power goals. The gastrocnemius necrosis finding is
specific to marathon-distance running, not necessarily to all forms of aerobic
conditioning used in team-sport contexts.

**Example** — **Inference:** programming continuous, moderate-pace circuit stations as a
"two birds, one stone" strength-and-conditioning solution is not well supported by this
evidence; separating a short conditioning block from resistance training, or using
interval-format circuits with real rest between high-intensity efforts, is the better-
supported approach.

**Related** — [[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force]].

Besides its role in ballistic and rapid movements, connective tissue can also increase the overall bulk of the muscle

For example, an insufficiently strong or extensive sheath of connective tissue will allow the muscle to dissi­

The connective tissues which are not structurally linked to the muscles, such as those in the ligaments, joint

moving parts and absorbing shock. The importance of this passive role should not be forgotten in overall 
training, since it is pointless to develop bulk and strength if the remainder of the musculoskeletal system is not 
equipped to handle the increased strength. One must condition muscle, bone and connective tissue if overall per­

produce a muscle complex which is prone to injury and inefficient in generating reactive strength. This is one 
reason why anabolic steroids are regarded as harmful: apparently they tend to hypertrophy and increase the 
strength of muscles relative to tendons, so that musculotendinous injuries are more common among steroid users.

(such as tendons, ligaments and joint capsules) or systems which contain a high proportion of connective tissue 
(such as bone and cartilage) only display significant adaptation and hypertrophy after several weeks or months of 
progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies, 1984). It is vital that the prescription of training takes into account the  
different rates of adaptation of all the systems involved  and avoids overtraining the systems with the slowest rates

preparation phase (GPP) and by relative novices to strength training.

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). Verkhoshansky states training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; he recommends gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)

**Why it works** — Muscle's adaptive machinery (protein synthesis, neural recruitment)
responds faster than the slower turnover and remodeling of collagenous tissue; a program
that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace what tendon, ligament,
and bone can structurally tolerate, which is a well-established mechanism in tendon and
connective-tissue injury research independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
athlete's tissue status or injury history.

**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
climbing.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

12	---
13	
14	# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops
15	
16	**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
17	training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
18	resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
19	and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
20	does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
21	adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
22	the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
23	training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
24	different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
25	different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
26	glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
27	dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
28	balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
31	synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
32	different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
33	model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
34	late and lost early.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
37	that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
38	hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
39	often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
40	systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
41	Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
42	adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
43	build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
44	Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
45	capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
46	underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
49	structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
50	without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
51	four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
52	it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
53	a specific testing checklist.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete returning from a multi-week layoff might show
56	CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
57	and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
58	either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
59	(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.
60	
61	**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

13	
14	# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept
15	
16	**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
17	to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
18	acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
19	the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
20	strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
21	peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
22	below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
23	cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
24	(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
25	anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
26	recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
27	circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
28	older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
29	or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
30	oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
33	physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
34	product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
35	rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
36	dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
39	classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
40	next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
41	framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
44	irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
45	marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
46	"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
47	corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
48	
49	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
50	more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
51	would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
52	"flushing out lactic acid."
53	
54	**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].
55

dunng weeks 12-20 was attributed to increased neural activation. In highly trained athletes, the increase in muscle 
hypertrophy is even more limited, thereby emphasizing the importance of using high intensity, rapid transition 
techniques for stimulating their nervous systems.

hypertrophy, and the lack of correlation between hypertrophy and strength gain stresses the futility of 
prescribing hypertrophy training for highly qualified athletes. This type of training is suitable for novices, but its 
regular use may be seriously detrimental to the strength and strength-specd performance of elite athletes.

low intensity for long periods during the same stage of a conditioning programme as strength training seriously 
compromises the development of strength and power. This is probably partly due to the fact that it is relatively 
easy for the faster twitching fibres to become or behave like slow twitch fibres with prolonged low intensity 
training. Furthermore, studies of the gastrocnemius muscles of distance runners have shown that prolonged 
distance training produces muscle necrosis and inflammation which can be detected at least 7 days after a 
marathon (Hikida et al, 1983). Comparative muscle biopsy studies of weightlifters, sprinters and rowers after 
strenuous training sessions do not show any of these abnormalities.

instructors and machine manufacturers maintain that continuous circuit training (CCT) regimes simultaneously 
develop cardiovascular endurance and strength. Research does not support this belief. On the contrary, it shows 
that it is more appropriate to prescribe cardiovascular training separately in limited amounts during the early off­
season and high intensity resistance training at a later stage. In addition, interval circuit training (ICT) using high 
intensity loading and regular rest intervals is more suitable for development of strength and strength-endurance.

ST (Type I) fibres are recruited first for muscle tensions up to about 25%, the FTa (Type IIA) are recruited next 
and the FT (FF or Type IIX) fibres last, as the intensity of the activity increases towards a maximum or as the ST 
fibres bccome seriously energy depleted (Fig 1.26). Therefore, if the intention is to train FT fibres for a particular 
sport, it is vital that high intensity training be concentrated upon.

maximum) or near IRM loads, but the degree to which the relevant muscle fibres are recruited during the effort.

exclusively FT fibres and slow movements ST fibres. To analyse the involvement of different fibre types, it is 
vital to determine the force that needs to be produced. If large acceleration of the load is involved, Newton's 
Second Law of Motion decrees that the resulting force will be large. Thus, the maximal force generated during 
rapid acceleration of a 100kg bench press easily can exceed the maximal force produced during a slowly accelerated 
150kg bench press. Both a small load accelerated rapidly and a heavy load accelerated slowly strongly involve the 
FT fibres. Likewise, explosive movements rely heavily on the action of FT fibres.

SUPERTRAINING
Figure 1.28 Force-Velocity curve for different types of jump (Bosco, 1982). In the squat jump, the contractile component of the 
muscle is primarily responsible for force production, whereas elastic energy plays a central role in dip (counter movement) jumps and 
depth jumping. The calculated values of F and V for high jump, long jump and sprints are also shown.
This figure also shows that jumping with a preliminary dip (or, counter movement) causes the F-V curve to shift 
upward away from the more conventional hyperbola-like F-V curve recorded under isokinetic conditions or with 
squat jumps. For depth jumps, the resulting graph displays a completely different trend where the force is no 
longer inversely proportional to the velocity of movement. The coordinates describing the more rapid actions of 
running, high jumping and long jumping also fall very distant from the traditional F-V curve.
The reason for these discrepancies lies in the fact that movement under isokinetic and squat jumping 
conditions involves mainly the contractile component of the muscles, whereas the ballistic actions of the other 
jumps studied are strongly facilitated by the release of elastic energy stored in the SEC during the rapid eccentric 
movement immediately preceding the concentric movement in each case (see 1.7.2).
Studies of F-V curves under non-ballistic and ballistic conditions (Bosco, 1982) further reinforces the above 
findings that the traditional F-V curves do not even approximately describe the F-V relationship for ballistic O f 
plyometric action (Fig 1.29). The theoretical basis for the traditional F-V curves is discussed in detail in Section 
3.3.2, but the non-applicability of these curves to ballistic motion should be carefully noted, especially if testing 
or training with isokinetic apparatus is being contemplated for an athlete.
Figure 1.29 Force-Velocity curves for concentric and ecccntric muscle contraction under different conditions (Bosco, 1982). Curve A 
refers to isolated muscles stretched at constant velocity by constant intensity electrical stimulation; curve B was obtained by isokinetic 
analysis of elbow flexion; curve C gives the F-V relationship for cccentric work produced by drop jumps from different heights.
Other work reveals that the jump height reached and the force produced increase after training with depth jumps 
(Bosco, 1982). Whether this is the result of positive changes in the myotatic stretch reflex, the structure of the 
SEC of the muscle or in both is not precisely known yet. What is obvious is that the normal protective decrease 
in muscle tension by the Golgi tendon organs does not occur to the expected extent, so it seems as if plyometric

input.old_string:
**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme (slow-twitch fibres recruited first up to
roughly 20% of maximum force, then progressively more fast-twitch fibres as force rises)
holds for graded, progressive loading, but Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp.
63-64) shows it breaks down for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over
700 N of vertical ground reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies
almost entirely on slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a
leg-press plate produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch
action. The force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic
testing reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional
hyperbolic F-V curve, while countermovement (dip) jumps and depth jumps are strongly
shaped by elastic energy released from the Series Elastic Component during the preceding
rapid stretch, producing an entirely different curve shape that does not fit the
traditional model. Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the
traditional F-V curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not
advisable for athletes in predominantly ballistic sports.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and
[[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force|this entry's]] own caution: SJ, CMJ,
and depth-jump testing are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality,
because they load the contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also
reinforces caution about isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already
raised in [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because it
directly overturns a simpler, still widely-taught recruitment model (force-graded,
slow-then-fast) using a small number of illustrative examples (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset; **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

# The Classic "Slow-Fibres-First-by-Force-Magnitude" Recruitment Model Fails for Ballistic Movement

**What it is** — The standard recruitment scheme (slow-twitch fibres recruited first up to
roughly 20% of maximum force, then progressively more fast-twitch fibres as force rises)
holds for graded, progressive loading, but Bosco (1982, cited PDF pp. 74-75, printed pp.
63-64) shows it breaks down for ballistic motion. Walking at moderate speed produces over
700 N of vertical ground reaction force yet, by contact time and movement pattern, relies
almost entirely on slow-twitch action; a maximal, high-velocity knee extension against a
leg-press plate produces less force than walking despite being nearly pure fast-twitch
action. The force-velocity curve itself differs by jump type: squat jumps and isokinetic
testing reflect mainly the muscle's contractile component and follow the traditional
hyperbolic F-V curve, while countermovement (dip) jumps and depth jumps are strongly
shaped by elastic energy released from the Series Elastic Component during the preceding
rapid stretch, producing an entirely different curve shape that does not fit the
traditional model. Sprinting, high jump, and long jump coordinates also fall far from the
traditional F-V curve. Bosco specifically cautions that isokinetic training is not
advisable for athletes in predominantly ballistic sports.

**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] and
[[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force|this entry's]] own caution: SJ, CMJ,
and depth-jump testing are not interchangeable measures of the same underlying quality,
because they load the contractile component and the SEC to very different degrees. Also
reinforces caution about isokinetic testing/training for ballistic-sport athletes already
raised in [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` rather than `supported` because it
directly overturns a simpler, still widely-taught recruitment model (force-graded,
slow-then-fast) using a small number of illustrative examples (walking, car-pushing,
seated knee extension) rather than a systematic dataset; **Inference:** treat the classic
graded model as a reasonable first approximation for slow, controlled movement, and this
critique as the more accurate account specifically for ballistic/SSC-involved movement.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach should not assume a squat-jump-based force
measurement predicts depth-jump or sprint ground-reaction performance; the elastic
contribution present in the latter two is largely absent from the former.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
late and lost early.

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), Verkhoshansky states biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first, oxidative ATP
resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle protein (myosin)
and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase; only after that
does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining or detraining, these
adaptations are lost in the reverse order they were gained. The longer the training period,
the more thorough the adaptation and the longer those biochemical changes persist after
training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels). This gain/loss asymmetry across
different systems is termed heterochronic (different tissues and processes change on
different timelines). Overtraining specifically shows a distinct pattern: reduced
glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/glycogen, blood plasma
dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to disrupted acid-base
balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity, structural protein
synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular mechanisms with
different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts, then de-adapts"
model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while others are gained
late and lost early.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
four-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist.

CP-system/power qualities holding up relatively better than the earlier-gained oxidative
and glycogen-storage qualities, or vice versa, depending on the specific loss sequence;
either way, "detraining" is not a single uniform decline and re-testing across qualities
(not just one) gives a more accurate readiness picture.

--- idx 87 (printed 76) ---
SUPERTRAINING
anabolic. Another group of reactions which is catabolic is cellular respiration,  whereby fatty acids, glucose and 
amino acids are broken down in the cells to release energy and form ATP.
All energy-requiring processes in the cells rely ultimately on the basic energy molecule of the body, ATP 
(adenosine triphosphate). This molecule consists of adenosine (a combination of adenine  and the sugar ribose) 
linked with three phosphate molecules by high-energy bonds, in particular the two outermost phosphate bonds 
(Fig 1.35). When the latter two bonds are broken, a burst of energy is released and the ATP is broken down to 
ADP (adenosine diphosphate). The ATP is applied directly to the muscle cross-bridges to activate and maintain 
the process of cross-bridging between the heads on the myosin filaments and the active sites on the actin filaments 
of the muscle fibres (see 1.7).
This energy is produced in the tiny mitochondria , the so-called 'powerhouses' of the cell, whose major 
responsibility is to power muscle contractions. These energy generators produce ATP only in the presence of 
adequate oxygen, so that there needs to be an emergency back-up system to generate ATP under oxygen deficient 
circumstances. Such a system, indeed, exists in the cells. It was mentioned above as the oxygen-independent 
glycolytic system. It depends on a group of enzymes or specialised biological catalysts which facilitate the 
oxygen-independent breakdown of stored glycogen and blood glucose in the cell and provide the necessary energy 
for muscle contraction.
The Concept of Oxygen Debt
Exercise under these conditions of high intensity effort is followed by a period of accelerated breathing, which 
used to be thought of as a mechanism employed to pay back an 'oxygen incurred by relying on non-oxidative 
processes and depriving the body of oxygen during the exercise. Nowadays, the concept of an oxygen debt is 
considered as outmoded. Instead, the post exercise period is now known to reflect recovery oxygen consumption 
to regenerate cellular ATP (and CP) and to return the respiratory, ionic, circulatory, hormonal and thermal pro­
cesses to their resting state (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991).
1.15.3 The Short-term Energy System
The energy for high intensity, high power or very rapid activity comes largely from the high energy phosphagen 
stores (ATP and CP). The initial energy is furnished by the breakdown of ATP into ADP and inorganic 
phosphate Pi in the presence of water and the enzyme adenosine triphosphatase  (Note: the suffix '-ase' refers to a 
compound serving as a biological catalyst to facilitate or control a biochemical reaction). Each mole of ATP 
produces about 7.3 kilocalories (35 kilojoules) of energy and a residue of ADP, which has to be upgraded to ATP 
from the CP (creatine phosphate) stores (Fig 1.35).
Figure 1J5 Energy processes involving ATP. ADP and CP
The small quantity of ATP in the muscle cells is depleted within a few seconds of strenuous all-out activity and 
muscle action would cease but for the fact that energy is transferred rapidly to the ADP by the CP reservoir in the 
cells. There is some three to five times as much CP as ATP in the cells, which enables the phosphagen system to 
fuel intense effort for a maximum of 20-30 seconds. The enzyme creatine kinase  catalyses this reaction. After 
this, the exercise intensity has to drop to enable the phosphagen stores to be replenished by the other energy
76


--- idx 89 (printed 78) ---
lactate is reconverted to pyruvate for use as an energy source. In addition, the lactate and pyruvate formed in 
muscle during exercise can be used to manufacture glucose by gluconeogenesis  ('neo-' means 'new'; ’-genesis' refers 
to ’making', so this word means 'making new glucose') in a process known as the Cori cycle.  This supplements 
any existing blood glucose and muscle glycogen.
Moreover, muscle fatigue  is not due to 'lactic acid poisoning' of the muscles. The formation of lactate (or 
lactic acid) is accompanied by the presence of positively-charged hydrogen ions (H+) or protons. These electrical 
charges, which increase the acidity of the blood, can interfere with the muscle contraction process and the 
efficiency of the enzymes involved in energy production. Neither should lactic acid be regarded as the cause of 
muscle soreness , since blood lactate levels return to normal within an hour or so of strenuous interval training.
Furthermore, the most pronounced muscle soreness occurs after prolonged endurance events performed at 
speeds which keep lactate levels below the lactate threshold. Current theories favour the explanation that the 
soreness is due to transient damage of muscle cells or connective tissue.
Hydrogen is released at various stages of glycolysis and transferred to another metabolic system, the electron 
transport chain , which employs iron-containing proteins called cytochromes  (in the mitochondrial membrane) to 
produce mitochondrial ATP. Oxygen ultimately combines with these hydrogens to form water, a major by­
product of metabolism, along with carbon dioxide produced by processes such as the Krebs cycle (Fig 1.36).
Lactate does not accumulate to a significant degree until exercise intensity reaches about 55% of the healthy, 
untrained subject's maximum capacity for oxidative metabolism. The rate of lactate accumulation now excecds its 
rate of removal and fatigue is initiated. The intensity of exercise has to be decreased if the activity is to continue. 
The point at which this occurs, formerly known as the anaerobic threshold, is now referred to as the blood lactate 
threshold  (or tumpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation).
The superior ability of the trained endurance athlete at higher levels of prolonged exercise intensity is largely 
due to the fact that:
• this threshold occurs at a higher percentage of one's oxidative (aerobic) capacity
• the athlete removes lactate more rapidly or converts it more efficiently to glucose.
It has also been proposed that lactate in one region of the working muscle of a trained athlete may be oxidised in 
the same or neighbouring less active muscles.
1.15.5 The Long-term Energy System
The long-term ('aerobic') energy system implicates metabolism under oxidative conditions and, as discusscd 
earlier, may use cither carbohydrates or fats to produce the necessary ATP for energy release in the muscles. 
Since all food carbohydrate is ultimately converted to glucose, carbohydrate metabolism may be understood in 
terms of glucose metabolism, a topic which was discussed earlier.
Protein sometimes may also be used as an energy source. After ingestion, the amino acids from the protein 
are stripped of their amine groups (NH 2) in a process called deamination and converted to pyruvate or other 
substances (keto acids), which can then enter the Krebs cycle (Fig 1.36).
The neutral fats (or lipids) which act as an energy source are triglycerides, which comprise a glycerol molecule 
to which are attached three fatty acid molecules. A process known as lipolysis  (Mipo-' means 'fat'; '-lysis' means 
'breaking down') breaks down the triglyceride into its constituent fatty acids and glycerol, via the intervention of 
the enzyme, triglyceride lipase. The fatty acids  then undergo beta oxidation,  a series of biochemical events which 
eventually produces acetyl CoA  for entry into the Krebs cycle. After processing via other mechanisms, the 
glycerol molecule may be converted to glucose or fed into the Krebs cycle.
It has been said that 'fats bum in a carbohydrate flame', since the combustion of fats in the body relies on an 
adequate supply of carbohydrates. When there is a carbohydrate deficiency, fat oxidation is incomplete and the 
liver converts the acetyl CoA into by-products called ketones , which are released into the blood stream. If these 
ketones accumulate faster than they can be used as fuel by the cells and large quantities are secreted in the urine, 
ketosis occurs. Since ketones generally are strongly acidic, the acidity of the blood increases markedly and 
metabolic acidosis becomes evident. The person's breath displays a fruity (or nail varnish) smell as acetone is 
released from the lungs and breathing accelerates. Untreated serious cases of metabolic acidosis can lead to coma 
and death.
SUPERTRAINING
78

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is** — Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
older term "anaerobic threshold" has similarly been replaced by "blood lactate threshold"
or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation) since lactate does not require an absence of
oxygen to form. (PDF pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.

**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related** — [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)

**Why it works** — The table estimates an average, whole-game contribution, whereas actual
play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays) separated by long rest (huddles,
substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real repeated-sprint, phosphagen-
dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role of aerobic recovery between
bursts.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky's own caution applies directly here: **Inference**
do not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown, and the source text itself flags the whole table's accuracy as needing
re-examination. This entry is rated `contested` because it is presented as a classic,
already-questioned scheme rather than an established modern reference.

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reproduces Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables estimating
the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). Verkhoshansky himself cautions that
this "highly determinate" scheme, compiled decades earlier, has been questioned, that
figures for some events (he names the 1500m specifically) have since been revised, and
that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment metabolic
demand shifts within a single sport. (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81.)

**Why it works** — The authors state these figures "reflect the average contributions made
by three concurrently operating metabolic systems ... for an average athlete," which
"disguises the fact ... that the metabolic demands often differ from instant to instant
during every type of activity taking place in each sport" (printed 81). Inference: for
football specifically, actual play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays)
separated by long rest (huddles, substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real
repeated-sprint, phosphagen-dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role
of aerobic recovery between bursts; the text does not itself apply this reasoning to
football.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own caution applies directly here: **Inference:** do
not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown. The text itself states that "the highly determinate nature of this whole scheme,
compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more recently" and that figures for
longer events "have been modified by other researchers" (printed 81). This entry is rated
`contested` beyond that self-flagged caution because modern measurement puts the aerobic
contribution far higher, and earlier in an effort, than these 1970s tables allow for (e.g.
Gastin, 2001, Sports Med 31:725-741).

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related** — None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

SUPERTRAINING
listening to dear descriptions of the kinesiology involved. This includes teaching complete movements and the 
same movements broken down into parts. Coaches and leading athletes are also expected to exhibit exemplary 
behaviour to enhance desirable learning by novices.
6. The Principle of Specialisation 
Here two aspects of specialised training are recognised:
(a) Practice in the specific sport under conditions which are encountered in competition. Competition is 
regarded as important in the learning of specialisation, so coaches advise regular participation in selected 
competitions.
(b) Special exercises for perfecting motor skills, tactics and other aspects essential to performing efficiently in 
the sport.
Many Russian experts claim that successful performance at an early age docs not necessarily ensure proficiency 
in adulthood. They consider that early specialisation is possible in sports such as gymnastics which emphasize 
coordination, agility, flexibility or speed, because of the pre-adolescent's particular ability in these respects. 
Strength and endurance sports are discouraged among youngsters. Research indicates that children should be 
admitted to sports schools according to the first column of Table 1.2, with higher levels of achievement being 
expected at the ages given in the last two columns.
The Russians recognise that there are individual exceptions, but they point out that the vast majority of their 
champions are adults. For instance, at recent Olympics the average age of Soviet participants has been about 24 
years, with more than half of them between 24 and 30, and fewer than 10% under the age of 20 years.
Early specialisation at an intense level does not seem to produce an enduring athlete, hence the importance of 
applying the guidelines provided in Table 1.2. Few athletes match the long spans of success enjoyed by 
weightlifters Alexeev and Rigert or pole-vaulter Bubko. Between 1970-78 Alexeev won 22 gold medals at World 
championships and Olympics, while Rigert won 17. The phenomenal Bubko broke numerous world records.
Table 1.2 Ages for starting, specialising and reaching high performance in different sports (in years).
Sport Begin the sport Specialisation age High performance
Basketball 7-8 10-12 20-25
Boxing 9-10 15-16 20-25
Cycling 9-10 16-17 21-24
Diving 5-6 8-10 18-22
Fencing 7-8 10-12 20-25
Figure skating 5-6 8-10 16-20
Gymnastics (women) 4-5 10-11 14-18
Gymnastics (men) 5-6 12-14 18-24
Rowing 12-14 16-18

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material — early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
specialization later draws on. Verkhoshansky's text does not itself restate this mechanism
in this passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a more granular, sport-by-sport reference
table alongside this library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric
detail beyond, the Bompa library's
[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
break it out by individual sport; this convergence is this entry's own comparison, not
stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table,
not a modern, population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies
(see [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football, not listed in Table 1.2 at
all) do not map cleanly onto these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as
illustrative, not prescriptive, for a Baylor Athletics context; this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — **Inference:** The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
in this library.

14	# A Minimum Load Threshold Drives Strength Gains, and It Rises as the Athlete Adapts
15	
16	**What it is** — Hettinger & Muller (1953) are cited for a threshold training stimulus of
17	roughly one-third of maximal strength needed to produce a strength increase in an average
18	person; as strength rises, the required stimulus intensity rises too, eventually reaching
19	80-95% of the athlete's maximum, sometimes matching or exceeding actual competition
20	intensity (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Each stimulus level has its own "strengthening
21	threshold," a ceiling beyond which no further gain occurs at that intensity, and this
22	ceiling is described as further from the untrained state the less trained the athlete is.
23	Separately, Korobkov, Gerasimov & Vasiliev (via Verkhoshansky, 1977) are cited for the
24	finding that in the initial stages of training, strength increases roughly uniformly
25	regardless of load, with approximately equivalent gains reported at 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%
26	of 1RM; raising training intensity early (heavier load, faster tempo, less rest) does not
27	reliably improve on this until strength has already progressed some way. (PDF pp. 33-34,
28	printed pp. 22-23.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — Early neuromuscular adaptation (see
31	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
32	any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
33	closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
34	ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription
37	simple and consistency-focused rather than chasing high intensities, and supports
38	progressively raising relative intensity toward 80-95% of max as an athlete's training age
39	increases, consistent with this book's own training-age-scaling heuristic
40	([[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]]).
41	
42	**When NOT to apply** — These are single-source, decades-old figures cited without a
43	stated sample or modern replication in this text (Hettinger 1961; Korobkov, Gerasimov &
44	Vasiliev via Verkhoshansky 1977; PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 22-23). **Inference:** do not
45	treat "one-third of max" or the specific 20/40/60/80% equivalence as precise, universal
46	cutoffs for a current athlete population; use them as a directional argument for why novice
47	programming can be simple, not as exact percentages to program from.
48	
49	**Example** — **Inference:** A true beginner's program built around consistent submaximal loading (e.g.
50	50-60% 1RM) can produce comparable early strength gains to a heavier protocol, so there is
51	little value in front-loading high intensity before the athlete has trained long enough to
52	need it.
53	
54	**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].
55

14	# High-Velocity Training Transfers to Low Velocity Better Than the Reverse; Contraction Modes Barely Cross Over
15	
16	**What it is** — Two specific, cited findings under the specificity umbrella: (1)
17	low-velocity isokinetic training improves low-velocity strength but has minimal effect on
18	high-velocity strength; high-velocity isokinetic training improves high-velocity strength
19	and transfers somewhat better to low-velocity strength than the reverse direction
20	(Moffroid & Whipple 1970; Perrine & Edgerton 1981; Kanehisa & Miyashita 1983b). (2)
21	Contraction-mode adaptations are narrow: concentric-eccentric (weightlifting-style)
22	training raises competitive strength but produces only small isometric or concentric
23	isokinetic gains; isometric training raises isometric strength but not concentric
24	isokinetic strength; elbow-extension training with weights increases triceps strength and
25	girth without a matching isokinetic-strength change. Static and dynamic training even
26	produce different microscopic structural changes in the muscle. (PDF pp. 38-40, printed
27	pp. 27-29.)
28	
29	**Why it works** — Force-velocity curve position (see
30	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
31	recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
32	structural adaptations underlie each; high-velocity training likely also recruits fast-
33	twitch units that contribute somewhat at slower speeds, which is the proposed reason the
34	transfer is asymmetric rather than symmetric.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,
37	match both to the sport action being targeted, and consider biasing toward higher-velocity
38	work when in doubt, since the text's cited data shows it transfers in both directions
39	somewhat, whereas slow, heavy work transfers poorly to fast actions. **Eric's baseline:**
40	the isometric seated calf raise and other isometric testing are run on the ForceDecks
41	"Mid-Thigh Pull" setting as part of the department's standard protocol
42	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
43	`protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md`, `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`). **Inference:**
44	this claim's contraction-mode specificity finding supports treating isometric testing as
45	its own distinct quality rather than a proxy for dynamic 1RM strength; neither source states
46	this connection directly.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** these are 1970s-1980s isokinetic-dynamometer
49	studies (PDF pp. 38-40, printed pp. 27-29); isokinetic machine training is a narrow,
50	lab-style modality rarely used in current collegiate S&C practice, and this specific
51	transfer asymmetry has not been independently re-verified here for free-weight or
52	plyometric training modes. **Inference:** do not assume the same asymmetric-transfer ratio
53	applies to, say, barbell velocity-based training without separate evidence; this extension
54	is not addressed in the text.
55	
56	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete tested for isometric mid-thigh pull strength should not be assumed
57	to have an equivalent dynamic 1RM or sprint force capability; each needs its own
58	assessment and, if targeted, its own specific training exposure.

13	
14	# The Voluntary-Involuntary Strength Reserve Has a Measured Size
15	
16	**What it is** — Two cited figures quantify how much force voluntary effort leaves
17	unused relative to the athlete's true ceiling. (1) In experienced weightlifters, the mean
18	gap between training maximum (TFmax) and competitive maximum (CFmax) is about 12.5 ± 2.5%,
19	larger in heavier weight classes (Zatsiorsky, 1995; PDF p. 13, printed p. 2). (2) Under
20	involuntary or hypnotic conditions, strength output can rise by up to 35% in untrained
21	people, but by less than 10% in trained athletes (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, no primary
22	citation given in text for this figure).
23	
24	**Why it works** — Both numbers describe the same phenomenon from different angles: a
25	protective neural inhibition normally holds voluntary output below the muscle's true
26	contractile ceiling, and anything that reduces that inhibition (competitive arousal,
27	hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of it. Training narrows the
28	untapped reserve because part of the strength-training adaptation is learning to
29	recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue.
30	
31	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why
32	max-effort numbers move around by context (weigh-in day nerves, meet atmosphere, testing
33	environment), and as a rough expectation that a smaller gap between training and
34	competitive/testing efforts is itself a marker of higher training status. Neither the
35	book nor Eric's baseline states this as an applied rule; it is this entry's own synthesis
36	of the two cited numbers.
37
