input.new_string:
**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
training algorithm" (`research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-
countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`), which independently argues against
using either of this book's two directions as a programming rule.

**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: SJ-vs-CMJ comparison on ForceDecks is a
modern, instrumented analogue of this book's proposed proxy, but given the book's internal
conflict and Kozinc et al. (2022)'s finding that the difference does not validate a
training algorithm, this entry gives no basis for deriving a training-emphasis rule from
that comparison.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this framework to set training emphasis from an
SJ/CMJ-style gap in either direction; the book contradicts itself on which direction is
which (printed 9-10), and the modern evidence on this specific test (Kozinc et al. 2022)
does not support a diagnostic cutoff or algorithm built on it. Use RSI, mRSI, or other
modern jump-testing metrics on their own validated basis instead of this 1990s-era
heuristic.

**Example** — Inference: no training-emphasis direction can be taken from this source; see
Kozinc et al. (2022) for the modern evidence on SJ-CMJ differences.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]],
[[research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip]].

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]). True Fmm
requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and risky to test directly. As a
field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from a static, knees-flexed start
(no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a sudden dip (a countermovement
that recruits the stretch reflex and involuntary/reactive contribution). A small
difference between the two jumps suggests the athlete is already recruiting most of their
available force voluntarily, i.e. training should emphasize raw force/strength capacity;
a large difference suggests a bigger untapped reactive/neural reserve, i.e. training
should emphasize "shock" and ballistic (reactive) methods instead. (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 9; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is credited to Zatsiorsky,
1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

**Why it works** — A countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and a degree
of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access; the size of the
resulting performance gap is a rough behavioral index of how much of the athlete's
reactive/neural potential is already expressed voluntarily versus still latent.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). **Inference:** comparing SJ height/output to CMJ
height/output for the same athlete is effectively running this framework's proposed
1993-2009-era proxy with instrumented, repeatable data instead of a stopwatch-and-tape
comparison; neither the book nor the baseline states this equivalence directly. **Inference:**
a small SJ-CMJ gap (or a low CMJ-to-SJ ratio) would, by this framework's logic, suggest
programming should lean toward raw strength/force development, while a large gap would
suggest more reactive-strength/shock-method work (depth jumps, plyometrics); this specific
programming inference is not stated in either source and would need independent
validation before use.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a directional heuristic from Verkhoshansky's text (PDF p.
20, printed p. 9), not a validated cutoff; no threshold percentage is given there for
"small" versus "large" gap. **Inference:** the modern jump-testing literature uses more
specific derived metrics (RSI, mRSI, eccentric utilization ratio) developed independently
of this 1990s framework, and those should be the primary interpretive tool; treat this
entry as a conceptual ancestor, not a replacement. **Inference:** do not use a single
SJ/CMJ comparison on one test day to make a training-emphasis decision; use trended data.
This trending caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the source text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete with SJ and CMJ heights within 1-2 cm of each other is a candidate
for a strength-emphasis block; an athlete with a large CMJ advantage over SJ (a high
eccentric utilization ratio) is more likely to respond to reactive/plyometric emphasis.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]].

# Strength Deficit Size Points to a Different Training Method

**What it is** — If an athlete's strength deficit (see
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]) is large for a given muscle
group, the text recommends near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (weightlifting or
plyometric methods) or, if very large, Compensatory Activation Training (CAT) with 5-8RM

**Why it works** — A large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural capacity
still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max effort
or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit means
the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further gains
require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express more
force.

explosive/team-sport athletes: for actions with little time to produce force (change of
direction, sprint push-off, jump takeoff), a large SJ/CMJ-style deficit would, by this

14	# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed
15	
16	**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
17	inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
18	constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
19	beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
20	high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
21	"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
22	different points on the curve. Critically, there is no correlation between an athlete's
23	maximal strength and their maximal velocity — they are described as different motor
24	abilities. (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky & Matveev 1964, Komi 1979,
25	Zatsiorsky 1995.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — The F-V relationship reflects the cross-bridge cycling and motor unit
28	recruitment limits of muscle contraction; it has been confirmed for whole-body sporting
29	movement as well as isolated muscle, and is the direct ancestor of the force-velocity
30	profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others) used in modern sprint and jump testing.
31	
32	**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
33	the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
34	speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
35	(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
36	the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
37	for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
38	force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.
39	
40	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
41	max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
42	speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
43	speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
44	development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
45	repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
46	"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
47	**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
48	prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
49	frameworks are equivalent. Verkhoshansky himself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as
50	not universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
51	force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
52	(Sutamo & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
53	not a universal law for every muscle group.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
56	different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
57	argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
58	heavy squatting to close it.

61	[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

13	
14	# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently
15	
16	**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
17	large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
18	acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
19	(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
20	under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
21	argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
22	neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
23	printed pp. 21-22.)
24	
25	**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
26	action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
27	the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
28	acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
29	several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
30	general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
31	text.
32	
33	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
34	solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
35	vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
36	mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
37	generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
38	comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).
39	
40	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
41	correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
42	non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
43	& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
44	how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
45	caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
46	
47	**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
48	clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
49	acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
50	coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
51	adaptation.
52	
53	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
54

14	# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size
15	
16	**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
17	increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
18	how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
19	hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
20	regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)
21	
22	**Why it works** — Hypertrophy is a slow structural adaptation; force output can rise
23	well before meaningful cross-sectional area change through improved recruitment,
24	firing rate, and coordination of the muscle already present. This is one of the more
25	independently replicated findings in strength physiology outside this text (early-phase
26	strength gains preceding measurable hypertrophy is a standard finding in resistance
27	training research), which is why this entry is rated `proven` rather than `supported`
28	despite the book being the citation vehicle here.
29	
30	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength
31	gains in novice athletes that outpace any visible muscle growth. **Eric's baseline:**
32	Tracy Fober's "use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" standard prioritizes
33	movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM
34	numbers, especially early in a training cycle (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
35	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`; `week1-lecture.md p.46`).
36	**Inference:** that coaching standard is consistent with this principle's emphasis on
37	coordination before load, though the baseline material does not itself cite the
38	neuromuscular-primacy mechanism. **Inference:** the same logic likely explains why
39	detraining strength loss can outpace measurable muscle loss (neural efficiency degrading
40	faster than tissue), though this text does not state that extension explicitly.
41	
42	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
43	on adequate muscle cross-section (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7), so hypertrophy is not
44	unimportant at higher training ages. **Inference:** this principle should not be used to
45	justify skipping hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window,
46	where structural gains matter more for continued strength progress; this caution is not
47	stated in the text itself.
48	
49	**Example** — **Inference:** A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
50	the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
51	predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
52	tissue growth.
53	
54	**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
55	mechanisms by which this happens).

12	---
13	
14	# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy
15	
16	**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
17	(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
18	following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
19	(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
20	delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
21	than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
22	increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
23	seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
24	elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
25	concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
26	storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
27	minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
28	dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
31	constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
32	is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
33	plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
34	the stretch magnitude is identical.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues
37	for minimizing ground-contact/amortization time in plyometric and reactive-strength work
38	(depth jumps, bounds, sprint ground contacts), and behind why reactive strength index
39	(RSI/mRSI, already the department's chosen daily readiness marker) is sensitive to contact
40	time as well as jump height — a longer amortization phase indicates the athlete is not
41	capturing the SSC benefit this mechanism describes.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the cited cross-bridge lifetime range (15-120ms) is
44	a cellular-level parameter, not a directly coachable or measurable field variable; do not
45	try to cue an athlete toward a specific millisecond target. Use it as the "why" behind a
46	qualitative cue (minimize ground contact time, avoid pausing at the bottom of a jump), not
47	as a number to program.
48	
49	**Example** — **Inference:** cueing an athlete to "spend as little time on the ground as
50	possible" during a depth jump, rather than pausing briefly before jumping, is a practical
51	application of keeping the stretch-to-shorten transition inside the cross-bridge
52	attachment window.
53	
54	**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
55	[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].
56

# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy

**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)

**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
the stretch magnitude is identical.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues
for minimizing ground-contact/amortization time in plyometric and reactive-strength work
(depth jumps, bounds, sprint ground contacts), and behind why reactive strength index
(RSI/mRSI, already the department's chosen daily readiness marker) is sensitive to contact
time as well as jump height — a longer amortization phase indicates the athlete is not
capturing the SSC benefit this mechanism describes.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the cited cross-bridge lifetime range (15-120ms) is
a cellular-level parameter, not a directly coachable or measurable field variable; do not
try to cue an athlete toward a specific millisecond target. Use it as the "why" behind a
qualitative cue (minimize ground contact time, avoid pausing at the bottom of a jump), not
as a number to program.

**Example** — **Inference:** cueing an athlete to "spend as little time on the ground as
possible" during a depth jump, rather than pausing briefly before jumping, is a practical
application of keeping the stretch-to-shorten transition inside the cross-bridge
attachment window.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].

--- idx 30 (printed 19) ---
SUPERTRAINING
For instance, although the presence of a high percentage of fast twitch muscle fibres in an athlete may suggest 
that the latter may be well suited to sports which require production of power and speed, the existence of any 
inherently disadvantageous limb leverages or techniques which do not optimise torque production in specific 
complex joint actions may decree that any muscle fibre advantage may be of diminished importance. 
Occasionally, however, a disproportionate increase in strength for a given activity may tend to offset these 
negative factors and enable the athlete to perform quite competently, albeit in a less efficient or economic manner.
Later the issue of torque for activities involving several joints will be examined to caution us against the 
casual analysis of joint action according to the standard methods of functional anatomy (Ch 3). We will then 
leam that we are not necessarily justified in assuming that a given muscle will produce the same joint action in a 
multi-joint task if the anatomy charts show that it produces a certain joint action (such as flexion) when only that 
joint is involved in the movement. We will also leam that, in multi-joint (multi-articular) tasks, a muscle may 
exert a profound effect over a joint which is not crossed by that muscle.
Earlier we saw that strength is not the maximal force (or torque) which a muscle can generate; that is actually 
maximal strength. Strength, as is consistent with the definition of force according to Newton’s Laws (see later), 
is simply the ability to generate force to overcome inertia or a load. Similarly, we can define concepts such as 
maximal torque and maximal power, as well as optimal torque and power (rate of doing work).
Possibly the best known curve in strength training is the hyperbolic Force-Velocity curve first described by 
Hill (Fig 1.9) that is widely used to reinforce the view that maximum force production can occur only at zero or 
very low velocities. This curve may be used to show the different effects of velocity-centred and force-centred 
training. Although this relationship originally was derived for isolated muscle, it has been confirmed for actual 
sporting movement, though the interaction between several muscle groups in complex actions changes some aspects 
of the curve (Zatsiorsky & Matveev, 1964; Komi, 1979).
This curve implies that velocity of muscle contraction is inversely proportional to the load, that a large force 
cannot be exerted in very rapid movements (as in powerlifting), that the greatest velocities are attained under 
conditions of low loading, and that the intermediate values of force and velocity depend on the maximal isometric 
force. It is misleading to take this to mean universally that large force cannot be produced at large velocities, because 
ballistic action involving stretch-shortening and powerful neural facilitation exist to manage such situations, as will 
be discussed later in more detail.
In addition, more recent research has shown that that the Force-Velocity relationship is not necessarily a 
continuous hyperbolic relationship during muscle shortening and that the commonly modelled force augmentation 
effect of muscle lengthening is incorrect, at least concerning submaximal activation of the lower back extensors 
(Sutamo & McGill, 1995). For instance, the erector spinae exhibit a yielding phenomenon which causes force to 
drop abruptly during constant velocity stretching under constant, submaximal stimulation. This study showed 
further that the eccentric behaviour of the lower erectors (lumbar level L3) appears to be independent of velocity 
and length, while that of the upper erectors (thoracic level T9) displays a dependence on length. At lower concentric 
velocities, a concavity in the Force-Velocity curves appeared after some sort of "threshold” velocity was exceeded.
Figure 1.9 The relationship between force and velocity, based on the work of Hill (1953). (a) The dark curve shows the change produced 
by heavy strength training. This situation refers to ‘strength-speed’ training, (b) The dark curve here shows the change produced by low 
load, high velocity training. This situation refers to ‘speed-strength’ training, (after Zatsioreky, 1995).
19


--- idx 31 (printed 20) ---
SUPERTRAINING
The influence of maximal isometric strength on dynamic force and velocity is greater in heavily resisted, slow 
movements, although there is no correlation between maximal velocity and maximal strength (Zatsiorsky, 1995). 
The ability to generate maximum strength and the ability to produce high speeds are different motor abilities, so that 
it is inappropriate to assume that development of great strength will necessarily enhance sporting speed.
The effect of heavy strength training has been shown to shift the curve upwards (as shown in Fig 1.9), 
particularly in beginners (Perrine & Edgerton, 1978; Lamb, 1984; Caiozzo et al, 1981) and light, high velocity 
training to shift the maximum of the velocity curve to the right (Zatsiorsky, 1995). Since, in both cases, power = 
force x velocity, the area under the curve represents power, so that this change in curve profile with strength 
increase means that power is increased at all points on the curve. The term ‘strength-speed' is often used as a 
synonym for power capability in sport, with some authorities preferring to distinguish between strength-speed  
(the quality being enhanced in Fig 1.9a) and speed-strength  (the quality being enhanced in Fig 1.9b).
Optimisation of force, torque, speed and power or the production of ‘just the right amount at the right time’ 
of these motor abilities sometimes seems to be forgotten, especially in the so-called strength, heavy or contact 
sports. All too often, the solution to most performance problems in such sports seems to be a philosophy of 
“the greater the strength and the greater the muscle hypertrophy, the better”, despite the fact that one constantly 
witnesses exceptional performances being achieved in these sports by lighter and less strong individuals.
The full ramifications of the concept of power often tends to be lost in Western strength training because the 
term “speed-strength”, directly translated from the Russian texts on strength training , is used as its colloquial 
equivalent. Thus, we encounter programmes on how to “increase power", which is entirely nebulous in the 
context of human movement, because the concept of power may appear in several different forms in 
biomechanics, namely ‘mean power’ (over a given interval), peak power (at some specific instant) and power at 
any given instant. Just as it is not very meaningful to develop maximal strength (force) or high mean force in 
every situation or stage of a movement, so it can be equally inappropriate to train an athlete to simply develop 
“power", irrespective of context. One of the central features of all motor skill is the ability to produce maximal 
power and power in the most efficient manner possible. In fact, all effective strength utilisation and training 
means optimally timing the magnitude of force, power and rate of force development (RFD) throughout any 
movement.
Since bodily motion is the result of muscle action and its underlying metabolic processes, one must 
distinguish between internal and external energy and work. Externally, assuming no losses by heat or sound, 
mechanical energy usually occurs in the form of potential energy (PE) and kinetic energy (KE), where PE is the 
energy possessed by a body by merit of its position and KE is the energy which a body has by virtue of its 
velocity.
Although external work is defined popularly as the product of the force and the distance through which it is 
exerted, this definition applies only if the force is constant and acts strictly along the path joining the starting and 
end points of the movement. The mathematical definition based on integral calculus generally is avoided in 
training texts, because it is felt that it may not be adequately understood by the practitioner, while the popular 
definition usually attracts the condemnation of the scientist, because of its limited applicability and scope. For 
this reason, a definition of work in terms of energy changes is given, namely:
Work W * Final Energy - Initial Energy' = Final (PE + KE) - Initial (PE + KJE)
Alternatively, we could draw a graph of how the force varies with displacement; then work would be given by the 
area under the curve between the starting and end points of the action (Fig 1.10).
Since some of the fundamental equations used to analyse sporting movements may be expressed in the form 
of suitable graphs, this same graphic approach may be adopted to enable us to visualise more simply the 
implications of biomechanics for training and competition. In this respect, the following relationships will be 
seen later to play an especially important role in the biomechanics of strength and power in sport:
• Force vs Time (or Torque vs Time)
• Force vs Displacement (and Torque vs Joint Angle)
• Force vs Velocity
• Rate of Force Development vs Time
20

# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is** — Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Critically, there is no correlation between an athlete's
maximal strength and their maximal velocity — they are described as different motor
abilities. (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky & Matveev 1964, Komi 1979,
Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works** — The F-V relationship reflects the cross-bridge cycling and motor unit
recruitment limits of muscle contraction; it has been confirmed for whole-body sporting
movement as well as isolated muscle, and is the direct ancestor of the force-velocity
profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others) used in modern sprint and jump testing.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. Verkhoshansky himself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as
not universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutamo & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example** — **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — Force alone does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle
action type, or motor unit recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect
the training stimulus; two efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-
acceleration combinations are mechanically equal on that one variable but different on
several others that matter physiologically. This is the mechanistic backbone of the
general specificity-of-training principle, which is well established independent of this
text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

SUPERTRAINING
training. For example. Cooper (1968: p25) stated that: “If it's muscles or a body beautiful, you’ll get it from 
weightlifting or calisthenics, but not much more... If it’s the overall health of your body you’re interested in, 
isometrics won’t do it for you, neither will isotonics or anaerobics. Aerobic exercises are the only ones that will.”
It was inevitable that the accompanying high profile marketing and media campaigns, extensively 
underwritten by the medical profession, would make the pursuit of strength oriented sports considerably less 
attractive in the public eye. Olympic Weightlifting became and still is a rarity in schools in the West and strong 
young men are steered more in the direction of sports such as American football and rugby, games which by mere 
acceptance into the school curriculum ensure a huge pool of talent.
During the same period, the Russians and Eastern Europeans accumulated extensive international information 
on strength and sports training while developing a vast research effort into these topics, as well as establishing a 
vast coaching and educational sports programme. Most schools offered weightlifting and within a few decades 
after World War II there were at least a million Olympic lifters in the USSR alone. Besides its application in 
competitive weightlifting, strength training became an integral part of all sports training in Russia, whereas in the 
West, the attitude more often was one which claimed that weight training slowed one down, made for unnecessary 
bulk and reduced flexibility. Quite predictably, Russia began to dominate the Olympic Games, especially in 
Olympic weightlifting, at the same time that the cardiovascular doctrine began to dominate the West.
This Russian dominance often has been simplistically attributed to the extensive use of drugs such as the 
androgenic-anabolic steroids, but, ironically, the synthesis and sporting use of these drugs was pioneered in the 
West. It is more accurate to state that the use of such drugs became equally extensive in East and West and that 
dominance in many international sports by Eastern nations was more a consequence of several other vital factors, 
especially strength science and organisational systems.
The West today would appear to have reaccepted a useful role for strength training, but the proliferation of 
weight training facilities and personal trainers still has much more to do with commercialism than the impact of 
strength science, as is emphasized by the fact that the cardiovascular doctrine still dominates the fitness conscious 
psyche, there are few schools which offer Olympic lifting and there are fewer competitive lifters than ever before.
The Modern Era Dawns
The systems of training of the early pioneers touched upon above ultimately formed the framework of modem 
competitive bodybuilding and weightlifting, with some of the exercise techniques and machines being adopted into 
physiotherapy and the coaching regimes for other sports. Yet, serious scientific research into strength training 
only developed well into the 20th century and, as we have seen, even now research into cardiovascular training 
attracts considerably more attention from scientists.
Nevertheless, the evolution of resistance training in several different directions has produced an invaluable 
data base from the following distinct sources (the details in parentheses refer to the purpose of each discipline):
• Weightlifting and powerlifting (competitive performance against maximal resistance)
• Bodybuilding (resistance training to maximise muscle hypertrophy)
• Supplementary resistance training (resistance exercise to enhance fitness in other sports)
• Physiotherapy (resistance exercise for rehabilitation)
• Scientific research (analysis to understand resistance exercise scientifically).
The information in this book is selected from the above sources to present an integrated approach to the use of 
strength training to enhance performance in all top level sport. Throughout, the approach has been to reconcile 
competitive lifting and sporting performance with scientific research, for theory without practice is as limited as 
practice without theory. It would be premature, however, to maintain that all questions in strength training have 
been answered: on the contrary, the quest for a definitive science and art of strength training is still in its infancy.
The Fundamental Principle of Strength Training
The production and increase of strength both depend on neuromuscular processes. Strength is not primarily a 
function of muscle size, but one of the appropriate muscles powerfully contracted by effective nervous 
stimulation. This is the foundation of all strength training.
Several centuries ago, when electricity, less still bioelectricity, was not of much scientific interest, this 
principle was already anticipated by Sir Isaac Newton, who wrote in his Principia Mathematica (1687) of "a

ccitain most subtle spirit which pervades and lies hidden in all gross bodies," and that "all sensation is excited, and 
the members of animal bodies move at the command of the will, namely, by the vibrations of this spirit, mutually 
propagated along the solid filaments of the nerves, from the outward organs of sense to the brain, and from the 
brain into the muscles." In other words, if we restate the terminology of those times, we will note that the central 
role of the mind and nervous system in human movement was already stressed by one of science’s leading figures.
In the 1930s, the New York strongman, Paul Boeckmann, stressed in his treatise. Nerve Force , the 
importance of the nerves in strength training, and considered nervous control, conservation of nervous energy and 
the ability to generate explosive force at the time of greatest need as the foundation of physical power (Paschall, 
1954). He also pointed out the great importance of using regular rest periods to enhance nervous recovery.
Physiology tells us that structure is determined by function, where muscle hypertrophy is an adaptive 
response to neuromuscular stimulation of a given minimum intensity. Thus, nervous stimulation produces two 
basic adaptive and interrelated effects in the body:
• functional muscular action (the functional effect)
• muscle hypertrophy (the structural effect).
The fundamental principle o f strength training, then, is that all strength increase is initiated by neuromuscular  
stimulation. Although hypertrophy is the long-term result of a certain regime of neuromuscular stimulation, it is 
not the inevitable consequence of all types of work against resistance. Two basic types of resistance training may 
be recognised, namely:
• functional resistance training
• structural resistance training.
In drawing up this distinction, it should be noted that there is no such thing as purely structural training, since all 
training is essentially functional, which, under certain conditions, may also elicit structural changes. Moreover, 
the production of maximal strength depends to a great extent on the existence of an optimal degree of muscle 
hypertrophy.
While structural resistance training is aimed primarily at producing muscle hypertrophy (and some aspects 
of tissue flexibility), functional strength training is associated with many different performance goals, including 
improvement in static strength, speed-strength, muscle endurance and reactive ability. In other words, the former 
produces increases in diameter and/or strength of individual muscle fibres, whereas the latter implicates the 
contractions of the numerous muscle fibres to produce the appropriate performance effect. At a more detailed 
level, functional training involves the following processes (Fig 1.2):
1. Intermuscular coordination  between different muscle groups. This involves the synchronisation or sequencing 
of actions between different muscle groups which are producing any given joint movements. Certain muscles 
may be inhibited from cooperating, while others may be disinhibited in contributing to the movement.
2. Intramuscular coordination  of fibres within the same muscle group. This implicates one or more of the 
following mechanisms of fibre control:
• Number encoding, the control of muscle tension by activating or deactivating certain numbers of fibres.
• Rate (frequency) encoding, the control of tension by modifying the firing rate of active fibres.
• Pattern encoding, the control of tension by synchronisation or sequencing of firing of the different types of 
muscle fibre (e.g. slow or fast twitch fibres).
3. Facilitatorv and inhibitory reflexive processes  in the neural pathways acting at various levels in the nervous 
system may be modified to optimise the development of strength, either by improving intra- and inter­
muscular coordination or by promoting adaptive changes in the various reflex systems of the body.
4. Motor learning, which is the process of programming the brain/central nervous system to be able to carry out
specific movement tasks (discussed in detail in 1.13). A great deal of the early improvement in strength and 
performance is a result of motor learning, this being vital to the continued efficiency of later training. Motor 
learning continues as the intensity and complexity of loading increases progressively, because skill under 
demanding conditions is significantly different from skill under less onerous circumstances.

SUPERTRAINING
The powerful influence of androgenic and anabolic steroids such as testosterone on muscle hypertrophy and 
function are well known, which has led directly to their huge abuse in sport. Less well known is the potent effect 
of thyroid hormone in this same regard. The first study to reveal this was conducted by Gold et al (1970), who 
showed that thyroid state influences the contractile properties of slow skeletal muscle. They found in rat soleus 
muscle that the hypothyroid state decreased the normal shortening velocity by 60%, while hyperthyroidism 
increased this velocity by 20%. Other work revealed that in the solcus muscle hyperthyroidism converts some 
slow  Type I fibres to Type IIA and IIX fibres and shifts the force vs frequency curve to the right (Caiozzo et al, 
1991). At the same time, hypothyroidism completely suppresses the expression of FT fibres in soleus. Even 
though soleus comprises only about 15% of FT fibres, this FT to ST conversion produces significant changes in 
the solcus force-frequency curve, which implies that the small relative population of FT fibres in soleus plays a 
vital role in determining the mechanical properties of this muscle (Caiozzo & Haddad, 1996). Thyroid state, 
however, has far less effect on FT muscles, such as plantaris (Caiozzo et al, 1991).
Hypothyroidism also retards the rate and extent of muscle growth, although the change in maximal muscle 
tension per unit cross-sectional area is insignificant. Another aspect of this work is the fascinating discovery that 
there appears to be a subset of the ST fibre group which is unresponsive to hormonal, mechanical or electrical 
stimuli and which have been called refractory Type I fibres (Caiozzo et al, 1993).

Moreover, rapid movements often recruit the muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex, which can elicit a powerful 
contraction. Relevant to this process is Starling's Law, which states that the strength of contraction is 
proportional to the original length of the muscle at the moment of contraction. The ideal relationship between 
tension and length in a sarcomere occurs when the muscle is slightly stretched and the actin and myosin filaments 
just overlap slightly. However, in applying this law, it has to be remembered that the advantage offered by the 
stretching may be diminished in cases where this stretching occurs at large joint angles which provide poor 
leverage. The well-known prestretch  principle in bodybuilding training and the plyometric method in speed- 
strength training rely on this phenomenon. Many gymnasium machines are seriously limiting in that they do not 
allow the user to begin a movement with a pre-stretch. Not only does this diminish the force which can be 
generated, but it also exposes joints to a greater risk of injury because the movement begins without muscular 
support for the ligaments.
The importance of the nervous system in developing strength cannot be ignored. As stated earlier, the 
development of strength is related to the number of appropriate muscle fibres firing simultaneously, which is 
entirely a function of the nervous system. An additional finding is that, if the nerve which normally supplies a 
ST muscle fibre is surgically interchanged (‘cross reinnervated’) with one which supplies a FT fibre, the ST fibre I 
will behave like a FT fibre (e.g. Bacou ct al, 1996; Baijot ct al, 1998). These studies, carried out on rabbits, suggest 
that sensitivity to motor innervation increases from the glycolytic to oxidative types of fibre, in the order: IIB > I 
IIX/IID > ILA> I (where the IID, like the IIB fibre types occur in small mammals as analogues of the human IK I 
type). In other words, the behaviour of muscic would appear to be determined by the activity of the nerve fibres I 
which supply it, a deduction which is discussed further in the next section.
The rate and number of fibres firing depends on voluntary and involuntary processes, the voluntary ones 
being related to personal motivation and biofeedback techniques, and the involuntary ones to feedback information , 
from the proprioceptive system, including the various stretch reflexes.
Thus, the simple act of motivating or emotionally willing yourself, through methods such as self-talk or 
guided imagery to produce greater or faster efforts can recruit a greater number of muscle fibres at an increased rate 
of firing. Encouragement by a training partner can also play a useful role in this regard, if done at appropriate 
stages during an exercise. Interestingly, the method of training with progressively heavier loads or at larger i 
accelerations is a valuable way of learning how to motivate yourself at progressively higher levels of performance

# Strength Increase Is Initiated by Neuromuscular Stimulation, Not Muscle Size

**What it is** — "The fundamental principle of strength training... is that all strength
increase is initiated by neuromuscular stimulation." Strength is framed as a function of
how powerfully and efficiently muscle is activated by the nervous system first, with
hypertrophy as a downstream, longer-term structural consequence of a given stimulus
regime, not the driver of early gains. (PDF pp. 17-18, printed pp. 6-7.)

**Why it works** — Hypertrophy is a slow structural adaptation; force output can rise
well before meaningful cross-sectional area change through improved recruitment,
firing rate, and coordination of the muscle already present. This is one of the more
independently replicated findings in strength physiology outside this text (early-phase
strength gains preceding measurable hypertrophy is a standard finding in resistance
training research), which is why this entry is rated `proven` rather than `supported`
despite the book being the citation vehicle here.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength
gains in novice athletes that outpace any visible muscle growth. **Eric's baseline:**
Tracy Fober's "use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer" standard prioritizes
movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM
numbers, especially early in a training cycle (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21`; `week1-lecture.md p.46`).
**Inference:** that coaching standard is consistent with this principle's emphasis on
coordination before load, though the baseline material does not itself cite the
neuromuscular-primacy mechanism. **Inference:** the same logic likely explains why
detraining strength loss can outpace measurable muscle loss (neural efficiency degrading
faster than tissue), though this text does not state that extension explicitly.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states maximal strength "depends to a great extent"
on adequate muscle cross-section (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7), so hypertrophy is not
unimportant at higher training ages. **Inference:** this principle should not be used to
justify skipping hypertrophy-phase work for athletes past the early-adaptation window,
where structural gains matter more for continued strength progress; this caution is not
stated in the text itself.

**Example** — **Inference:** A freshman who has never lifted seriously often adds meaningful strength in
the first 4-6 weeks of a program with little visible size change; that gain is
predominantly neural (coordination, recruitment, reduced antagonist co-contraction), not
tissue growth.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (the
mechanisms by which this happens).

# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff, change of
direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary force. An
athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still underperform in
short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached. This
distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well established
in modern force-time curve analysis, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver

# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is** — Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works** — Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well
established in modern force-time curve analysis outside this text, which the text itself
does not cite.

which explains why ruptures are more common in muscle than in tendon (Elliott, 1967).
These facts are directly relevant to appreciating the difference between static, passive and ballistic modes of 
stretching, with slow and rapid loading rates having different effects on the each of the soft tissues of the body 
(see 3.5.8).
The Role of Stored Elastic Energy
To superficial analysis it would appear as if dynamic contraction of the muscles of the arms and legs during 
activities such as running would account for a considerable amount of the expenditure of energy. Conversely, it 
has been found that the energetic cost of running for animals with heavy limbs is about the same as those with 
light limbs. This is the case because much of the energy involved is stored from step to step as elastic energy in 
the tendons (Goldspink, 1978). Throughout this process there is significant change in length of the tendons, but 
not in the muscle itself.
During active movement, the mcchanical energy stored in the PEC is small and contributes little to the energy 
balance of exercise. Conversely, considerable storage of energy storage can occur in the SEC during dynamic 
exercise, since an actively contractcd muscle resists stretching with great force, particularly if the stretching is 
imposed rapidly. The tendons play a major role in storing this energy. Explosive rebound (plyometric) training 
can have a significant cffcct on the SEC.
Whereas the SEC is implicated in activity when the muscle is contracted, the PEC exerts tension passively 
when the unstimulated muscle is stretched. The contribution of the PEC to total muscle tension increases with 
muscle length, a finding which is most relevant to integrating flexibility conditioning into an all-round 
strengthening programme.
The traditional view of tendons serving to attach muscic to bone presents only part of the picture. Tendons, 
together with other series elastic components, particularly after termination of powerful isometric or eccentric 
contractions, play a vital role in storing elastic energy during locomotion and other motor acts, thereby saving 
energy and increasing muscular efficiency.
For example, it has been found that much of the muscle activity in running is associated with tensioning of the 
lendons, which thereby store energy for successive cycles of movement (Cavagna, 1977). This tensioning or 
rewinding of the tendon fibres by largely isometric muscic contractions is achieved with very little change in the 
length of the muscle fibres themselves. The fact that the forces involved are derived mainly from isometric 
contractions means a decreased energy expenditure because isometric contractions thermodynamically arc 
considerably less expensive than dynamic contractions. For these reasons, it is important that any stretching 
manoeuvres do not compromise the strength or ability of the tendons to store elastic energy throughout their 
range of movement (see 3.5.8). This implies again that tendon stretching exercises should be accompanied by 
strength conditioning against adequate resistance. Similarly, ligaments should not be overstretched to the point of 
diminished joint stability.
The ability to use stored elastic energy depends on the velocity of stretching, the magnitude of the stretch 
and the duration of the transition between termination of the eccentric and initiation of the eccentric phases of the 
movement. This delay between the two phases should be minimal or the stored elastic energy will be rapidly 
dissipated, because a more prolonged delay will allow fewer cross-bridges to remain attached after the stretch 
lEdman ct al, 1978). Moreover, the greater the velocity of stretching during the eccentric contraction, the greater 
the storage of clastic energy (Rack & Westbury, 1974).
The increase in positive work associated with rapid eccentric-concentric (or plyometric) contractions is 
usually attributed to the storage and utilisation of clastic energy, but some of this enhanced work output is 
probably caused by pre-loading (or, pre-stretch) of the muscle complex. This is due to the fact that, during an 
impulsive eccentric-concentric action, the tension at the beginning of the concentric contraction is much greater 
than if the contraction had started from rest.
The Influence of Exercise on C onnective Tissue

**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)

# A Short Transition (Amortization) Between Stretch and Shortening Preserves Stored Elastic Energy

**What it is** — Actin-myosin cross-bridges have a limited lifetime, 15-120 milliseconds
(Edman et al., 1978). For stored elastic energy from a stretch to be used in the
following concentric contraction, the transition period between the end of the eccentric
(stretch) phase and the start of the concentric (shortening) phase must be brief; a longer
delay lets cross-bridges detach and the elastic potential dissipates as slippage rather
than being used for work. A greater velocity of stretch during the eccentric phase also
increases elastic energy storage (Rack & Westbury, 1974). Much of the extra positive work
seen in rapid eccentric-concentric (plyometric) actions is attributed to this stored
elastic energy plus a separate pre-loading/pre-stretch effect (tension at the start of the
concentric phase is already elevated by the preceding stretch). Tendon-based elastic energy
storage during locomotion largely happens via near-isometric muscle contraction with
minimal muscle fibre length change, which is also more metabolically efficient than
dynamic contraction. (PDF pp. 55-56, printed pp. 44-45.)

**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
the stretch magnitude is identical.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues
for minimizing ground-contact/amortization time in plyometric and reactive-strength work
(depth jumps, bounds, sprint ground contacts), and behind why reactive strength index
(RSI/mRSI, already the department's chosen daily readiness marker) is sensitive to contact
time as well as jump height — a longer amortization phase indicates the athlete is not
capturing the SSC benefit this mechanism describes.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the cited cross-bridge lifetime range (15-120ms) is
a cellular-level parameter, not a directly coachable or measurable field variable; do not
try to cue an athlete toward a specific millisecond target. Use it as the "why" behind a
qualitative cue (minimize ground contact time, avoid pausing at the bottom of a jump), not
as a number to program.

**Example** — **Inference:** cueing an athlete to "spend as little time on the ground as
possible" during a depth jump, rather than pausing briefly before jumping, is a practical
application of keeping the stretch-to-shorten transition inside the cross-bridge
attachment window.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]],
[[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]].

14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
23	factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
24	skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
25	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
28	muscular systems together (see
29	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
30	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
31	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
32	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
33	adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
34	conditioning research, independent of this text.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
37	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
38	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
39	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
40	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
41	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
42	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
43	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
44	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
45	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
46	chapter does not itself state that link.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
49	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
50	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
51	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
52	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
53	such in this passage of the text.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
56	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
57	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
60	[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].
61

14	# Strength Expression Depends on Torque Management, Not Just Load
15	
16	**What it is** — Torque (force times the perpendicular distance from the force's line of
17	action to the joint fulcrum) determines effective loading on a joint, independent of the
18	absolute weight lifted. Bringing a load closer to a joint reduces the torque at that
19	joint for the same weight: flexing the elbows reduces shoulder torque during dumbbell
20	raises/flyes/bench press; keeping a bar close to the body during the clean or deadlift
21	reduces torque at the lumbar spine and hips, allowing a heavier load to be lifted more
22	safely. Swinging the bar away from the body during a snatch pull, or a javelin away from
23	the shoulder during wind-up, are cited as inefficient uses of torque. (PDF pp. 28-29,
24	printed pp. 17-18.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
27	weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
28	which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.
29	
30	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis
31	tool for any lift where the bar or load can drift away from the body's midline (clean,
32	snatch, deadlift, overhead press) or away from a joint (dumbbell raises, flyes); keeping
33	the load's path close to the relevant joint is both a safety cue and a load-capacity cue.
34	This general coaching application is this entry's own extension of Verkhoshansky's
35	worked examples (PDF pp. 28-29, printed pp. 17-18).
36	
37	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanical principle about joint
38	loading, not a complete safety framework; it does not account for tissue tolerance,
39	technique proficiency, or fatigue-related form breakdown on its own, and the text does
40	not claim that it does. **Inference:** reducing joint torque is not always desirable if
41	the goal is specifically to overload that joint's musculature for rehabilitation purposes
42	(e.g., some hip- or shoulder-isolation rehab work intentionally increases moment arm at a
43	target joint under controlled load); this rehab caveat is not addressed in this section of
44	the text.
45	
46	**Example** — **Inference:** Cueing an athlete to keep the bar against the shins and thighs during a
47	clean pull, rather than swinging it forward, reduces lumbar torque for the same bar
48	weight and is both a technique and a load-management fix.
49	
50	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].
51

14	# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again
15	
16	**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
17	(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
18	begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
19	counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
20	load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
21	reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
22	rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
23	very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
