# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again

**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)

**Why it works** — This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

25	(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
26	level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
27	not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
28	(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic

# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky lists the factors that determine how much strength a
muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
printed pp. 33-34.)

**Why it works** — This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
rather than assuming a training-volume problem).

firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
factors alone.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

14	# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production
15	
16	**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
17	interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
18	distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
19	recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
20	(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
21	**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
22	influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
23	act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
24	scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
25	joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
26	perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
27	vs. peripheral, discussed further in
28	[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
29	12-13.)
30	
31	**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
32	volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
33	history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
34	not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
35	an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.
36	
37	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
38	underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
39	cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
40	state. Verkhoshansky states "return to top level performance will occur only if the
41	athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
42	minimal (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
43	in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and
44	Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
45	role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
46	`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
47	"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
48	**Inference:** Verkhoshansky's fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
49	that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
52	protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
53	of the text (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp. 12-13). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
54	as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
55	clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
56	look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
57	text.
58	
59	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
60	reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
61	and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
62	next intervention should target.
63	
64	**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].
65

1.4 Specificity in Training
The main reason why the prescription of resistance training for enhancing sports performance is not at all 
straightforward is that strength training displays definite specificity in many respects. This is the reason why the 
term 'sport specific strength training' is emphasized in this book: all forms of strength training are different and 
produce significantly different effects on ncuromuscular performance.
Fitness training for a given sport is not simply a matter of selecting a few popular exercises from a 
bodybuilding magazine or prescribing heavy squats, power cleans, leg curls, bench press, circuit training, 
isokinetic leg extensions or 'cross training'. This approach may produce aesthetic results for the average non­
competitive client of a health centre, but it is of very limited value to the serious athlete. It is not only the 
exercise which modifies the body, or, more specifically, the neuromuscular system, but the way in which the 
exercise is performed. In this regard, it is vital to remember that all exercise involves information processing in the 
central nervous and neuromuscular systems, so that all training should be regarded as a way in which the body's 
extremely complex computing systems are programmed and applied in the solution of all motor tasks (among its 
many other roles).
For many years, there have been two opposing theories of supplementary strength training in sport. One 
theory proposes that strength training should simulate the sporting movements as closely as possible with regard 
to movement pattern, velocity, force-time curve, type of muscle contraction and so forth, whereas the other 
maintains that it is sufficient to train the relevant muscles with no regard to specificity. Separate practice of 
technical skills would then permit one to utilise in sporting movements the strength gained in non-specific 
training. While both approaches to strength training will improve performance, current scientific research 
strongly supports the superiority of the specificity principle in at least ten respects:
• Type of Muscle Contraction • Muscle Fibre Recruitment
• Movement Pattern • Metabolism
■  Region of Movement • Biochemical Adaptation
• Velocity of Movement • Flexibility
• Force of Contraction • Fatigue
In the context of training, specificity should not be confused with simulation.  Specificity training means exercising 
to improve in a highly specific way the expression of all the above factors in a given sport. While simulation of a 
sporting movement with small added resistance over the full range of movement or with larger resistance over a 
restricted part of the movement range may be appropriate at certain stages of training, simulation of any 
movement with significant resistance is inadvisable since it can confuse the neuromuscular programmes which 
determine the specificity of the above factors.
Even if one is careful to apply simulation training by using implements or loads that are similar to those 
encountered in the sport, there will usually be changes in the centre o f gravity, moments of inertia, centre of  
rotation, centre ofpercussion and mechanical stiffness of the system which alter the neuromuscular skills required  
in the sport.. Features of the different specificity factors arc discussed briefly below.
Specificity of Type of M uscle C ontraction
Increases in voluntary strength are largely specific to the type of muscle contraction used in training. For 
example, the concentric-eccentric training of weightlifting increases competitive strength considerably, but 
produces only a small gain in isometric strength (Dons ct al, 1979; Thorstensson et al, 1976) or concentric 
isokinetic strength (Fahey & Brown, 1973). Concentric isokinetic exercise increases isokinetic strength and 
power without a noticeable increase in isometric strength (Kanehisa & Miyashita, 1983a). Conversely, isometric 
training markedly increases isometric strength, but not concentric isokinetic strength (Lindh, 1979). Elbow 
extension training with weights increases triceps strength and arm girth, but isokinetic testing of the same muscles 
reveals no significant change (Sale & MacDougall, 1977).

# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions

**What it is** — Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
mimicking a sport movement with added resistance is not the same as training the specific
factors above, and can actually distort the neuromuscular programming needed for the real
skill because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)

**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. This is one of the more broadly replicated findings in strength and
conditioning research, independent of this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
chapter does not itself state that link.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
such in this passage of the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]].

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. Verkhoshansky states "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** Verkhoshansky's fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);
**psychological factors** (motivation, focus, pain tolerance, perceived exertion, coach
influence); **pain and fear of pain** (distinguishing injury pain, a protective signal to
act on, from effort pain, a subjective load-intensity signal usable via an RPE-style
scale); **injury and fear of injury** (reflex inhibition of contraction around a damaged
joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
12-13.)

**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output,
not just "mental" factors layered on top of a physical ceiling — reflex inhibition around
an injured joint is a measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output
underperforms their apparent physical capacity: before assuming a physical/programming
cause, rule out fear of re-injury, unaddressed effort-pain tolerance, or psychological
state. Verkhoshansky states "return to top level performance will occur only if the
athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being
minimal (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13). **Eric's baseline:** Applied Performance's stated role
in return-to-performance is to supply information supporting Athletics Performance's and
Athletic Medicine's RTP decisions, a support/advisory role rather than a final-decision
role (`method-baseline.md`, "Rehab and return to play," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as
"the thinnest discipline in the corpus" with no stated RTP criteria or battery.
**Inference:** Verkhoshansky's fear-of-injury/pain framing is a plausible partial fill for
that documented gap, though neither source states this connection directly.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a descriptive taxonomy, not a measurement
protocol; none of these seven factors have a given cutoff or test threshold in this section
of the text (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp. 12-13). **Inference:** do not use "fear of injury"
as a catch-all explanation without other supporting evidence (movement quality, self-report,
clinical input from Athletic Medicine); reflex inhibition and psychological guarding can
look similar from the outside. This caution is this entry's own judgment, not stated in the
text.

**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete cleared medically after an ACL reconstruction who still shows
reduced force output on the operated leg during testing may be exhibiting reflex inhibition
and/or fear of re-injury, not a residual physical deficit alone; that changes what the
next intervention should target.

**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

14	# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training
15	
16	**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
17	targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
18	performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
19	ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
20	synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
21	control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
22	encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
23	facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
24	execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
25	some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — Force output for a given movement is the product of both how much
28	contractile tissue exists (structural) and how effectively the nervous system recruits,
29	times, and sequences that tissue (functional). Early or stagnation-phase training gets
30	more return from the functional side because coordination has more room to improve;
31	structural change is slower and more load-dependent.
32	
33	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states functional stages should precede structural
34	stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
35	8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
36	diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
37	structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
38	coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
39	framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.
40	
41	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
42	diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
43	plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
44	is coach judgment, not a test result. Verkhoshansky's use of "functional training" here
45	means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
46	**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
47	(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
48	address.
49	
50	**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
51	intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
52	insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
53	fix.
54	
55	**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

13	
14	# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition
15	
16	**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
17	initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
18	faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
19	(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
20	Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
21	swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
22	same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
23	research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
24	found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
25	and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
26	that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
27	high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
28	performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
29	restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
30	every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
31	pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
34	after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
35	(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
36	a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
37	competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.
38	
39	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
40	of this library's already-captured practical rule
41	([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
42	more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
43	scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
44	coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
45	volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
46	date.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
49	must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
50	periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
51	fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
52	swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
53	football or other team sports without independent verification.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
56	keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
57	deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
58	competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
59	shorter fatigue effect clears.
60	
61	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
62	[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].
63

13	
14	# Skilled Movement Depends on the Kinaesthetic System, and Is Shaped by Mental Rehearsal Before It Starts
15	
16	**What it is** — Skilled movement relies on the kinaesthetic sense, built from four
17	subsystems: joint receptors (joint angle and rate of change), muscle spindles (muscle
18	length and tension), the Golgi tendon apparatus (tension monitoring, protects against
19	excessive loading by reducing tension past a critical value), and the vestibular apparatus
20	(head/body position, velocity, acceleration), plus touch and pain receptors.
21	Proprioception is described as second only to pain in producing the most intense and
22	widespread brain electrical activity. Separately, research (Evarts 1973, 1979; Siff 1977)
23	found that the motor cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia all become active before a
24	movement begins, not merely in response to it as classically assumed; a specific 9 Hz "mu
25	rhythm" brain pattern is blocked in advance of movement. The cerebellum corrects and
26	reorganizes motor commands before they reach the muscles (feedforward control) and can
27	coordinate movement even without peripheral feedback; the motor cortex governs the amount
28	and pattern of muscular contraction. Russian training practice uses visualization (watching
29	film of top athletes/coaches, mental rehearsal) and autogenic training (imagining the full
30	sensory and emotional experience of competition, sometimes monitored with ECG/EMG/GSR) to
31	exploit this pre-movement brain activity. (PDF pp. 81-83, printed pp. 70-72.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Because motor planning measurably begins before the muscles act,
34	rehearsing a movement mentally (with vivid sensory and emotional detail) engages some of
35	the same preparatory neural circuitry as physically performing it, giving visualization a
36	plausible mechanism beyond simple relaxation or confidence-building.
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports including structured visualization/mental
39	rehearsal as a real training tool, not just a "soft skill," for technical rehearsal (e.g.
40	before a max-effort lift or a technical skill) and pre-competition routines. Also useful
41	teaching framework for explaining to athletes and students (e.g. HHPR 5355) why
42	proprioceptive/joint-position training (balance, landing mechanics, reactive drills) is
43	foundational to skill, not a separate "prehab" category.
44	
45	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** visualization/autogenic training is presented here
46	as a supplement integrated with physical practice, not a substitute for it; the text does
47	not claim mental rehearsal alone produces motor learning without physical repetition. The
48	detailed neuroanatomical claims (specific roles of basal ganglia vs. cerebellum, the mu
49	rhythm) are cited to 1970s research and should be treated as illustrative of the general
50	feedforward principle rather than as current, precise neuroscience.
51	
52	**Example** — **Inference:** having an athlete mentally rehearse a technical lift or a
53	competition scenario in vivid sensory detail before attempting it live is a direct,
54	practical application of this feedforward research, not just a motivational exercise.
55	
56	**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].
57

13	
14	# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
17	technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
18	another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
19	name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
20	don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
21	"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
22	movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
23	throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
24	and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
25	be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
26	requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
27	isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
28	joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
29	action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
30	range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
31	hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
32	printed pp. 49-53.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
35	(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
36	full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
37	terms track what is actually held constant and where.
38	
39	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
40	dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
41	the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
42	underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
43	isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
44	precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
45	distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
48	claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
49	what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
50	usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
51	convention.
52	
53	**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
54	a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
55	keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.
56	
57	**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].
58

# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
convention.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 60-80 |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works** — Each goal loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently:
near-maximal loads at low reps bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength);
high-velocity submaximal loads bias rate of force development (power); moderate loads at
moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads
at very high reps bias oxidative/metabolic endurance.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
baseline material does not cite Verkhoshansky's specific terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states this chart is "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 22, printed p.
11), and ignores the other prescription variables covered in
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] and later chapters. **Inference:** do
not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
football or other team sports without independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)

**Why it works** — Force output for a given movement is the product of both how much
contractile tissue exists (structural) and how effectively the nervous system recruits,
times, and sequences that tissue (functional). Early or stagnation-phase training gets
more return from the functional side because coordination has more room to improve;
structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states functional stages should precede structural
stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.

# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)

**Why it works** — The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply** — The authors state functional stages should precede structural
stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.

diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete

means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
address.

**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by

# Skilled Movement Depends on the Kinaesthetic System, and Is Shaped by Mental Rehearsal Before It Starts

**What it is** — Skilled movement relies on the kinaesthetic sense, built from four
subsystems: joint receptors (joint angle and rate of change), muscle spindles (muscle
length and tension), the Golgi tendon apparatus (tension monitoring, protects against
excessive loading by reducing tension past a critical value), and the vestibular apparatus
(head/body position, velocity, acceleration), plus touch and pain receptors.
Proprioception is described as second only to pain in producing the most intense and
widespread brain electrical activity. Separately, research (Evarts 1973, 1979; Siff 1977)
found that the motor cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia all become active before a
movement begins, not merely in response to it as classically assumed; a specific 9 Hz "mu
rhythm" brain pattern is blocked in advance of movement. The cerebellum corrects and
reorganizes motor commands before they reach the muscles (feedforward control) and can
coordinate movement even without peripheral feedback; the motor cortex governs the amount
and pattern of muscular contraction. Russian training practice uses visualization (watching
film of top athletes/coaches, mental rehearsal) and autogenic training (imagining the full
sensory and emotional experience of competition, sometimes monitored with ECG/EMG/GSR) to
exploit this pre-movement brain activity. (PDF pp. 81-83, printed pp. 70-72.)

**Why it works** — Because motor planning measurably begins before the muscles act,
rehearsing a movement mentally (with vivid sensory and emotional detail) engages some of
the same preparatory neural circuitry as physically performing it, giving visualization a
plausible mechanism beyond simple relaxation or confidence-building.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports including structured visualization/mental
rehearsal as a real training tool, not just a "soft skill," for technical rehearsal (e.g.
before a max-effort lift or a technical skill) and pre-competition routines. Also useful
teaching framework for explaining to athletes and students (e.g. HHPR 5355) why
proprioceptive/joint-position training (balance, landing mechanics, reactive drills) is
foundational to skill, not a separate "prehab" category.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** visualization/autogenic training is presented here
as a supplement integrated with physical practice, not a substitute for it; the text does
not claim mental rehearsal alone produces motor learning without physical repetition. The
detailed neuroanatomical claims (specific roles of basal ganglia vs. cerebellum, the mu
rhythm) are cited to 1970s research and should be treated as illustrative of the general
feedforward principle rather than as current, precise neuroscience.

**Example** — **Inference:** having an athlete mentally rehearse a technical lift or a
competition scenario in vivid sensory detail before attempting it live is a direct,
practical application of this feedforward research, not just a motivational exercise.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

If no sensory or proprioceptive feedback is implicated, the mode of control is termed feedforward  or 'open- 
loop' control (Smith & Smith, 1962; Green, 1967). Here, control is preprogrammed into the central nervous and 
ncuromuscular systems by the visual and auditory systems before movement begins, so that ongoing monitoring 
mechanisms arc not involved. The first sign of impending programmed action is the inhibition of antagonist 
contraction preceding agonist action, as revealed by the electromyograph. Premature activation of the antagonists 
may not only diminish skill, but it can cause muscle injury. During ballistic and other rapid movement, antagonist 
contraction is appropriate only to terminate further motion of the limb concerned. Not only is there no antagonist 
activity during ballistic movements, but it is also absent during discontinuous motion (Brooks, 1983). The 
advantage offered by feedforward processes is speed of action, whereas its main disadvantage is the lack of 
flexibility which can be offered by feedback. Nevertheless, the importance of feedforward processes in human 
movement should not be underestimated, as implied by the Russians in using regimes of visualisation and 
autogenic training in sports preparation.

14	# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)
15	
16	**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
17	Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
18	(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
19	expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
20	preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
21	stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
22	process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
23	base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
24	pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
25	derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
26	strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
27	flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
28	skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
29	separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
30	102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
33	four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
34	combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
35	sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
36	which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
37	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
38	neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.
39	
40	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
41	naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
42	"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
43	plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
44	"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
45	combinable qualities.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
48	descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
49	factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
50	**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
51	each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
52	standard test attached in this text.
53	
54	**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
55	(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
56	precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
57	weight-class or position-limited athlete.
58	
59	**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
60	[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

13	
14	# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)
15	
16	**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
17	hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
18	added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
19	of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
20	an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
21	cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
22	decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
23	itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
24	important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
25	near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
26	sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
27	(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
28	fibres. (PDF pp. 77-78, printed pp. 66-67.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
31	contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
32	existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
33	depending on the loading style that stimulated them.
34	
35	**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
36	measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
37	proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
38	is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
39	Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
40	biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
41	(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
42	for a specific position.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
45	stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
46	still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
47	biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
48	model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
49	produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.
50	
51	**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
52	might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
53	volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
54	lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.
55	
56	**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]].
57

13	
14	# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)
15	
16	**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
17	contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
18	cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
19	Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
20	carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
21	usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
22	stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
23	training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
24	stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
25	(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle; FT
26	fibres store more elastic energy overall. Static/relaxed/passive stretching mainly loads
27	the PEC; tensed/active stretching (and PNF techniques) load both the SEC and PEC. (PDF
28	pp. 51-52, printed pp. 40-41.)
29	
30	**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
31	given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
32	passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
33	tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
34	postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.
35	
36	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
37	training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
38	simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
39	active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.
40	
41	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
42	explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
43	functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
44	map to test or measure directly in an athlete.
45	
46	**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's calf (fast, elastic, SEC-dominant) and a
47	postural trunk muscle (slower, stiffer, PEC/collagen-dominant) would, by this model, be
48	expected to respond differently to the same static-stretch dose, supporting muscle-specific
49	rather than uniform flexibility prescription.
50	
51	**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
52	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
53

14	# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
17	speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
18	store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
19	jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
20	loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
21	reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
22	the eccentric phase. Historically, in the original Russian nomenclature, "pliometric"
23	referred specifically to eccentric (lengthening) contraction, distinct from "isometric"
24	(static) and "miometric" (concentric, shortening); the term "plyometrics," as adopted in
25	the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of jumping drills, many of which do
26	not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. Verkhoshansky's preferred precise
27	definition: an eccentric contraction suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric
28	contraction, producing a powerful myotatic reflex and a rapid extension of the muscle's
29	passive components, followed by an explosive concentric contraction. (PDF p. 45, printed
30	p. 34.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — The stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation plus
33	elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
34	independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
35	precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
36	ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.
37	
38	**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
39	exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
40	to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
41	predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
42	This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
43	[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
44	Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
45	method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
46	so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
49	current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
50	shock-method mechanism; Verkhoshansky himself notes this drift and recommends "shock
51	method" or "depth jumps" as the more precise Russian-tradition terms (PDF p. 45, printed
52	p. 34). This terminology distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or
53	appropriate for a given athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.
54	
55	**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
56	check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
57	transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
58	different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.
59	
60	**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
61	[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
62	(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the original
63	Russian terminology split — isometric/miometric/pliometric — and the precise mechanical
64	definition of the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).
