SUPERTRAINING
Antonio considers that the question which needs to be asked is not whether muscle fibre hyperplasia actual!; 
occurs, but rather under what conditions it does occur. The prolific amount of evidence which shows that increas 
in muscle mass most commonly is associated with an increase in muscle cross-sectional area certainly emphasize 
that hyperplasia does not take place as a simple matter of course, but under very special conditions which warran 
further research.
Although the existence of hyperplasia of muscle fibre may be uncertain or rare, hyperplasia o f structures  
within the muscle fibre and cell docs occur.  Nikituk and Samoilov (1990) identify two types of subfibral 
hyperplasia:
• Sarcoplasmic hyperplasia^  which involves an increase in the number of sarcoplasmic organelles
• Myofibrillar-mitochondrial hyperplasia , which involves increase in the number of myofibrils and
mitochondria.
Increase in muscle diameter is due to enlargement of individual muscle fibres by an increase in the number and size 
of individual myofibrils (Goldspink, 1980), accompanied by an increase in the amount of connective tissue 
(McDonagh & Davies, 1984), as discussed in Section 1.6. This increase in muscle protein is produced by 
increased protein synthesis and decreased protein degradation (Goldberg et al, 1975). Two types of muscic 
hypertrophy may occur (Fig 1.30):
• Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy.  In this case, the volume of non-con tractile protein and semifluid plasma between 
the muscle fibres increases. Although the cross-sectional area of the muscle increases, the density of muscle 
fibres per unit area decreases and there is no corresponding increase in muscle strength.
• Sarcomere hypertrophy.  Here there is an increase in the size and number of the sarcomeres which comprise 
the myofibrils. These may be added in series or parallel with the existing myofibrils, although only the 
parallel growth will contribute to an increased ability to produce muscic tension. The area density of 
myofibrils increases and there is a significantly greater ability to exert muscular strength.
Except for a few sports, such as bodybuilding and sumo wrestling, in which an increased bodymass without 
greater relative strength may contribute to performance, sarcomere hypertrophy is far more important than 
sarcoplasmic hypertrophy in most athletic activities.
The exact biochemical mechanism whereby hypertrophy is stimulated by resistance training is not yet known 
and existing theories are incorrect or incomplete (McDonagh & Davies, 1984). Post-exercise enhancement of 
protein synthesis has been attributed variously to triggering by ATP depletion, altered blood acidity, muscic 
hypoxia or rebound increase in blood circulation after intense contractions, but none of these mechanisms is 
adequately supported by research.
Figure 1.30 The different types of muscle fibre hypertrophy
Although not thoroughly corroborated, the energetics theory o f muscle hypertrophy  appears to be more acceptablc 
than the other theories, especially as seriously depleted ATP levels have not been detected even in completely 
exhausted muscles and changes in blood or nutrient flow have not been shown to stimulate muscle growth. This 
theory proposes that hypertrophy results from the ‘supercompensation' of protein synthesis after high intensity 
exercise, analogous to the supercompensation of muscle glycogen after prolonged lower intensity exercise.
66


--- idx 78 (printed 67) ---
SUPERTRAINING
Sincc glycogen supercompensation is a transient effect, lasting only long enough to facilitate prolonged 
aercise in endurance events, it is relevant to refer to our later remarks on the use of the term adaptive  
reconstruction instead of supercompensation (see 1.16).
The acute shortage of cellular energy after strenuous activity is held to be the trigger for the eventual 
aipercompensation (or adaptive reconstruction) during the subsequent low intensity or rest phases. Since each 
cell possesses only a fixed quantity of energy at any given instant, it has to be distributed between protein 
metabolism and mechanical work. Under conditions of rest or recovery, most of the energy is directed to protein 
synthesis, whereas most of it is devoted to muscic contraction during intense exercise (Fig 1.31). The lack of 
energy for protein growth and maintenance during heavy exercise apparently produces protein catabolism 
(breakdown), which stimulates protein supercompensation during later rest periods.
The prescription of any type of resistance training to producc a given functional change depends on 
examining the concurrent effects of the training regime on muscle hypertrophy and subfibral hyperplasia. The 
popular view is that the greater the intensity of the load, the greater the activation of the motor apparatus, so that 
the intensity offunctioning of structures (IFS) and hence, the amount of active muscle tissue grows. This is 
supported by the fact that muscle genes are regulated largely by mechanical stimulation (sec 1.12). Despite 
abundant earlier research indicating that intense physical loading apparently causes sarcomere hypertrophy, more 
recent findings, however, reveal quite the opposite result (Nikituk & Samoilov, 1990).
The data shows that the longer and more strenuous the submaximal loading (but not the rapid, near maximal 
low-rcpetition loading of Olympic weightlifting), the less there is sarcomere hypertrophy and the more there is 
sarcoplasmic hypertrophy. Although increase in load intensity and speeding up of its rate of increase promotes 
overall muscle hypertrophy, it is accompanied by a greater breakdown of muscle fibres and a decrease in the 
number of contractile structures. The hypertrophied muscle contains fewer sarcoplasmic organelles, myofibrils 
and mitochondria, so that the increased diameter of the muscle fibres is due largely to an increase in the volume of 
sarcoplasm (i.e. sarcoplasmic hypertrophy).
Figure 1.31 The distribution of cellular energy during intense resistance exercise versus rest. Note that prolonged intense resistance 
work can diminish the availability of energy for protein synthesis and halt any increase in hypertrophy of the muscle fibres.
Other research has found that hypertrophied muscle fibres need a significantly larger tissue volume to perform a  
given quantity of work. With the development of non-fiinctional hypertrophy, the increase in muscic mass 
outstrips the development of the vascular system. This results in diminished nutrition and oxygenation of the 
muscle, slowing down of metabolic processes in the muscle and less efficient disposal of metabolic waste 
products from the musculoskeletal system (Zalessky & Burkhanov, 1981).
Furthermore, adaptation occurs more slowly in connective tissue  (such as tendons and ligaments) than in 
muscic and any increased tension made possible in the musculotendinous complexes by the increased muscle mass 
can cause damage to these structures (Zalessky & Burkhanov, 1981). Thus, excessive hypertrophy usually leads to  
slower muscle recovery after exercise, deterioration in speed, speed-strength and speed, as well as an increased  
incidence of injury.
This might suggest that all muscic fibre hypertrophy lowers work capacity. Hypertrophy is an adaptive 
response to physical stress and does offer the benefit of increased mitochondrial surface area, which provides for 
more efficient energy processes than would an increased number of mitochondria. With a rapid increase in 
loading, the size of the mitochondria continues to increase markedly, but their number decreases and the 
concentration of ATP drops, thereby diminishing the partial volume of the contractile myofibrils. The resulting 
energy deficit soon inhibits the formation of new structures and the decreased amount of ATP stimulates various
67


--- idx 79 (printed 68) ---
SUPERTRAINING
destructive processes associated with decrease in the number of myofibrils. This process is referred to as 
irrational adaptation.
Growth of any living structure is related to the balance between its volume and its surfacc area. When muscle 
hypertrophy occurs, the surface of the fibres grows more slowly than their volume and, according to Hartwig and 
Mezia, this imbalance causes the fibres to disintegrate and restructure in a way which preserves their original 
thermodynamic state (Nikituk & Samoilov, 1990). It would appear that light and medium increases in loading 
require less energy, facilitate cell repair, minimise the occurrence of destructive processes and stimulate the 
synthesis of new, non-hypertrophicd organelles. Medium loads applied with a medium rate of increase in loading 
produce intense muscular development, the process in this case being referred to as rational adaptation.
The fact that conventional isometric training improves performance in static, rather than dynamic, exercise 
may be due to the different structural effects of isometric training. Gudzia has discovered that static training 
produces the following changes: the sarcoplasmic content of many muscle fibres increases, myofibrils collect into 
fascicles, nuclei become rounder, motor end-plates expand transversally relative to the muscle fibres, capillaries 
meander more markedly, and the layers of endomysium and perimysium thicken. In the case of dynamic training. 
the transverse striations of the myofibrils become very pronounced, the nuclei become oval and fusiform (spindle- 
shaped), motor end-plates extend the length of the muscle fibres, and the layers of endomysium and perimysium 
become thinner (Bondarchuk ct al, 1984).
The above work seems to corroborate the hypothesis referred to earlier that there may be an optimum size  
for muscle fibres undergoing hypertrophy  (MacDougall et al, 1982; Tesch & Larsson, 1982). The importance of 
prescribing resistance training regimes which produce the optimal balance between hypertrophy and specific 
strength then becomes obvious. Thus, it is not only prolonged cardiovascular training which can be detrimental to 
the acquisition of strength, but multiple fairly high repetition sets of heavy bodybuilding or circuit training rou­
tines to the point of failure may also inhibit the formation of contractile muscle fibres.
Therefore, it is vital to monitor regularly changes in muscular structure and function alongside changes in size 
and mass. In most cases the taking of biopsies is not possible or financially practical, so that indirect assessment 
of the adaptive processes is necessary. Increase in hypertrophy of a given muscle zone may be assessed from 
muscle girth and skinfold thicknesses at that site, while factors such as relative strength, maximal strength and the 
strength deficit (discussed early in Ch 1) serve as useful indicators of functional efficiency.
Bosco (1982a) cautions against the indiscriminate use of resistance training that typifies much of the 'cross 
training' prescribed with weights and circuits by Western personal trainers and coaches. He emphasizes that, 
although heavy resistance training serves as a powerful stimulus for the development and hypertrophy of both ST 
and FT fibres, the invaluable role played by FT development can be impaired by the accompanying growth of ST 
fibres, because the latter appear to provoke a damping effect on FT contraction during fast movement. This is 
due to the fact that, during high speed shortening of muscle, the sliding velocity of ST fibres can be too slow and 
therefore, may exert a significant damping effect on the overall muscle contraction. He concludes that the central 
role played by the storage and release of elastic energy by the connective tissues of the muscle complcx should 
never be ignored in sport specific training programmes (sec 1.7.2 and 5.2.4).
Effects of High versus Moderate Intensity Exercise
Besides the adaptive effects of the different regimes of strength training discussed above, there arc other effects 
worthy of mention which refer to the different outcomes produced by high intensity versus moderate or 
submaximal resistance training.
Besides enhancing muscle hypertrophy, low volume high intensity resistance exercise also increases the 
cross-sectional area of fast and slow twitch fibres, with a greater relative hypertrophy occurring in the fast-twitch 
fibres (McDougall et al, 1980; Tesch et al, 1985; Thorstennson, 1976). A comparison of strength- and 
endurance-trained subjects revealed that the area of both fast and slow twitch muscle fibres was greater in the 
strength-trained group (Alway et al, 1988). Tesch ct al (1987) showed that a six month-long, heavy resistance 
training resulted in a decrease in the activity of enzymes involved in 'aerobic' metabolic pathways (hcxokinasc, 
creatine kinase, myofibrillar ATPase, citrate synthase, myokinase and phosphofhictokinase). Other research 
revealed that citrate synthase activity is lower in weightlifters and powerlifters than in bodybuilders and non­
athletes (Tesch, 1988). This difference is probably due to the fact that wcightlifters and powerlifters regularly 
train at near maximal intensity with few repetitions, whereas bodybuilders train at moderate intensity and fairly
68


--- idx 80 (printed 69) ---
SUPERTRAINING
high volume. Five months of heavy resistance exercise was also shown to significantly increase the levels of the 
energy substrates glycogen, ATP, creatine phosphate and creatine (MacDougall et al, 1977).
Moderate intensity, high repetition resistance exercise, as commonly used in bodybuilding and circuit 
training, can also convert fast-twitch to behave more like slow-twitch fibres, apparently in an adaptive attempt to 
resist the fatigue of the repeated efforts (Timson et al, 1985; Baldwin et al, 1992; Noble & Pettigrew, 1989). 
Under these conditions, the transitional muscle fibres exhibit contraction times similar to those of fast fibres, but 
w ith fatigue resistance more like slow fibres. Thus, the capacity for strength-endurance seemed to increase.
A mechanism for this muscle adaptation was offered by Hoy et al (1980), who found that the fast isoforms 
of myosin disappear and are replaced by isomyosins that are characteristic of slow muscle after chronic 
overloading. This fibre transformation caused by chronic stimulation is regulated primarily at the genetic 
transcriptional level of regulation (Heilig & Pette, 1983). This process is associated with the presence in fast- 
tuitch muscle of a myosin light chain component that is usually observed only in slow-twitch fibres (Samaha et 
al, 1970). For these reasons, it would appear that high volume, moderate resistance training is actually high 
intensity, general endurance training.
Several studies of male and female bodybuilders have discovered that female muscle appears to adapt to 
resistance training in a different way from male muscle (Bell & Jacobs, 1990; Alway et al. 1992). Although the 
cross-sectional area of fast and slow twitch muscles increased in both male and female bodybuilders, the fast- 
twitch muscles of the males had a significantly greater area than the slow-twitch muscles, a trend which was not 
found among the females.
1.14 Neurophysiological Aspects of Exercise
All-round preparation of the athlete necessitates physical and psychological training, not as separate components, 
but as closely interrelated aspects of human performance. The mental and physical systems interact continuously 
and it is vital to remember that the highly-skilled, superbly conditioned body is of little value in competition 
without the right frame of mind. For instance, an emotional upset can prevent the athlete from relaxing or 
concentrating to produce the necessary degree of physical efficiency. Similarly, a slight physical injury may 
disturb one sufficiently to diminish confidence, concentration and skill.
The body may be viewed as a living cybernetic (control and communication) system in which the central 
nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord, controls the functions of the body via two major 
communication systems: the nervous system (autonomic and voluntary systems) and the hormonal system 
(endocrine glands).
The hormonal system is involved with control of the slower bodily processes such as growth, metabolism, 
sexual function, excretion and temperature regulation. The nervous system is concerned mainly with rapid 
processes such as sight, hearing, thinking and muscular contraction. However, these two systems interact in 
numerous processes, the link between them being the hypothalamus, situated near the middle of the brain. The 
hypothalamus is linked with the brain's limbic system (intimately connected with emotion) and the pituitary 
gland (sometimes called the master gland of the body). It may be inferred immediately that physical efficiency 
«i;pends on proper utilisation of thought processes, emotions and muscles.
This may be seen from Figure 1.32 which illustrates how external stimuli from the environment and internal 
stimuli from within the body are received by the specialised transducers of the sensory systems and relayed to 
the relevant parts of the central nervous system for further processing. Not only does the latter system activate 
the muscular system to produce appropriate patterns of movement, but it also relays information to the 
hypothalamus which may produce emotional and glandular responses.
Tbs model offers a simplified foundation for the psychology of sport. The remainder of this section is devoted to 
analysing the different systems of the body and applying this information to physical training and competition.
1. The Sensory System
The sensory systems (see Fig 1.32) provide man with information about his environment and his body. The 
traditional view refers to the 'five senses' (sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste), but neglects the vital 'inner 
senses' known as the kinaesthctic sense (sense of the position and movements of the body and its limbs) and the 
visceral sense (sense of operation of the inner organs such as heart and digestive system).

The hormonal system is involved with control of the slower bodily processes such as growth, metabolism, 
sexual function, excretion and temperature regulation. The nervous system is concerned mainly with rapid 
processes such as sight, hearing, thinking and muscular contraction. However, these two systems interact in 
numerous processes, the link between them being the hypothalamus, situated near the middle of the brain. The 
hypothalamus is linked with the brain's limbic system (intimately connected with emotion) and the pituitary 
gland (sometimes called the master gland of the body). It may be inferred immediately that physical efficiency 
«i;pends on proper utilisation of thought processes, emotions and muscles.
This may be seen from Figure 1.32 which illustrates how external stimuli from the environment and internal 
stimuli from within the body are received by the specialised transducers of the sensory systems and relayed to 
the relevant parts of the central nervous system for further processing. Not only does the latter system activate 
the muscular system to produce appropriate patterns of movement, but it also relays information to the 
hypothalamus which may produce emotional and glandular responses.
Tbs model offers a simplified foundation for the psychology of sport. The remainder of this section is devoted to 
analysing the different systems of the body and applying this information to physical training and competition.
1. The Sensory System
The sensory systems (see Fig 1.32) provide man with information about his environment and his body. The 
traditional view refers to the 'five senses' (sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste), but neglects the vital 'inner 
senses' known as the kinaesthctic sense (sense of the position and movements of the body and its limbs) and the 
visceral sense (sense of operation of the inner organs such as heart and digestive system).

# Sarcomere Hypertrophy (Functional) vs. Sarcoplasmic Hypertrophy (Non-Functional)

**What it is** — Two distinct types of muscle hypertrophy are described. Sarcomere
hypertrophy: an increase in the size and number of sarcomeres within myofibrils; when
added in parallel (not just in series) this increases the muscle's cross-sectional density
of contractile tissue and produces a real increase in strength. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy:
an increase in the volume of non-contractile protein and semifluid plasma between fibres;
cross-sectional area increases, but the density of contractile tissue per unit area
decreases, with no corresponding strength increase. Except in sports where added bodymass
itself matters (bodybuilding, sumo), sarcomere hypertrophy is described as far more
important for athletic performance. Longer, more strenuous submaximal loading (not rapid,
near-maximal, low-repetition loading like Olympic weightlifting) is associated with more
sarcoplasmic and less sarcomere hypertrophy; high-repetition, moderate-resistance training
(bodybuilding/circuit-style) can also make fast-twitch fibres behave more like slow-twitch
fibres. (PDF pp. 77-78, printed pp. 66-67.)

**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
depending on the loading style that stimulated them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add
measurable muscle mass/girth from high-volume, moderate-load training without a
proportionate strength increase, and why weightlifting-style low-rep, high-intensity work
is more strength-efficient per unit of added mass than bodybuilding-style volume training.
Useful framing for a strength coach deciding whether a hypertrophy block should be
biased toward heavier, lower-rep work (sarcomere-biased) or higher-volume work
(sarcoplasm-biased), depending on whether the goal is functional strength or added bodymass
for a specific position.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the exact biochemical trigger for hypertrophy is
stated in the text as not fully known, and this sarcomere/sarcoplasm distinction, while
still commonly discussed, has not been definitively confirmed by direct human
biopsy/histology consensus in the broader literature since; treat it as a useful coaching
model, not a settled biochemical fact, and don't claim a specific training protocol
produces "only" one type of hypertrophy in isolation.

**Example** — **Inference:** a lineman training for added mass and positional strength
might justifiably include both rep ranges, but should not assume high-rep hypertrophy
volume alone will translate proportionally into functional strength gains without
lower-rep, higher-intensity work also present in the program.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]].

All muscle comprises a contractile component, the actin-myosin system, and a non-contractilc component, 
the connective tissue. In mechanical terms, muscle may be analysed further (according to Levin & Wyman, 
1927) in terms of a contractile component in series with a series elastic component (SEC) and in parallel with a 
parallel elastic component (PEC), as illustrated in Figure 1.19. Although the anatomical location of these 
elements has not been precisely identified, the PEC probably comprises sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, 
and tissues such as the sheaths around the muscle and its sub-units. On the other hand, the SEC is considered to 
include tendon, the cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin filaments and the Z-discs. Of these elements, the 
myofilaments apparently provide the greatest contribution to the SEC (Suzuki & Sugi, 1983).
Figure 1.19 A simple mechanical model of the muscle complex
The PEC is responsible for the force exerted by a relaxed muscle when it is stretched beyond its resting length, 
whereas the SEC is put under tension by the force developed in actively contracted muscic. The mechanical 
energy stored by the PEC is small and contributes little to the energy balance of exercise (Cavagna, 1977). On the 
other hand, considerable storage of energy occurs in the SEC, since an actively contractcd muscle resists stretching 
w  ith great force, particularly if the stretching is imposed rapidly. This resistive force, exerted at the extremities of 
the muscle, and not the direct lengthening of contracted muscic, is responsible for the storage of elastic energy 
within the SEC.
Furthermore, it has been shown that mechanical strain imposed by stretching a contracted muscle is smaller in 
a muscle with a preponderance of ST (slow twitch) fibres, whereas the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres 
(Komi, 1984). The same study has also suggested that the elasticity of the SEC in a slow muscle is greater than 
that in a fast muscle. These differences are largely due to the fact that the concentration of collagen is higher in 
slow muscle than in fast muscle (Kovanen et al, 1984). Such findings agree with basic analysis of slow and fast 
movements. The high stiffness and low strain of a slow muscle clearly is most appropriate for muscle function 
which is intended for continuous support of posture. Conversely, the lower stiffness, greater compliance and 
lower elasticity of a strongly contracting fast muscle is eminently suited to enhancing speed and efficiency of 
movement. Further research has indicated that the differences in mechanical properties between fast and slow 
muscles in response to passive stretching are to a large extent due to their contcnt of collagcn.
In addition to the differences regarding the collagenous component of muscle, there are also differences in 
terms of the muscle fibres. Apparently ST fibres may be able to sustain cross-bridge attachments for longer 
penods than FT fibres. Therefore, prolonged muscle contraction would tend to be more easily maintained in slow 
postural (tonic) than in fast (phasic) musclcs. Consequently, stretching procedures would have to be applied for 
longer periods on slow muscles to significantly enhance their flexibility.
The muscic fibres can also stretch passively and store elastic energy, like tendons. In this respect, the myosin 
cross-bridges that are considered to pull the actin filaments between the myosin filaments during muscle 
contraction, arc known to be compliant structures which may stretch considerably before they detach from the 
activated sites on the actin filaments. It is believed that this compliance may be caused by rotation of the 
meromyosin heads of the cross-bridges and by elongation of its tail, which appears to have a helical structure that 
would promote extensibility (Huxley, 1974). In other words, even a contracted muscle can stretch, not only due 
to its collagenous component, but also due to its contractile tissue.
As stated earlier, if a relaxed muscle is stretched beyond its resting length, it is the PEC which appears to be 
most exposed to the resulting tension, whereas in active muscle it is the SEC which is subjected to most tension. 
This implies that static, relaxed ballistic and passive stretching have the greatest effect on the PEC, while tense 
ballistic and active stretching affects predominantly the SEC. The various physiotherapeutic PNF (Proprioceptive 
Neuromuscular Facilitation) flexibility techniques appear to be able to stretch and strengthen both the SEC and

F urther Inform ation on C ollagenous Tissue
The connective tissues comprise essentially three types of fibre, namely collagen, elastin and reticulin, with the 
former two fibres constituting approximately 90% of the whole. The collagen fibres (of which there are at least 1 0  
distinct types) impart strength and stiffness to the tissue, the elastin provides compliancc or extensibility under 
loading, and reticulin furnishes bulk (Fung, 1981). The elastic fibres occur in small concentrations in the 
intercellular matrix of tendons and most ligaments, but their function is not entirely clear. It has been suggested 
that they may play a role in restoring the crimped collagen fibre configuration after stretching or musck 
contraction (Minns et al, 1973).
The behaviour of the collagenous tissues in response to mechanical stress depends on the structural 
orientation of the fibres, the properties of the collagcn and elastin fibres, and the relative proportions of collagen 
and elastin. The structural orientation of the fibres differs for the various collagenous tissues and is specifically 
suited to the functions of each tissue.
In particular, the tendon fibres are closely packed and virtually parallel, but for a slight waviness in tk 
relaxed state. This simplicity of structure suffices for tendon, since the latter usually has to transmit force} 
linearly from one point to another. In ligaments and joint capsules the fibre organisation, though still generally 
parallel, is less uniform and often oblique or spiral, its exact structure depending on the function of the particular 
ligament. Most ligaments arc purely collagenous, the only elastin fibres being those which are associated with the 
blood vessels. Virtually the only ligaments which arc mostly elastin are the ligamentum flavum of the human spine 
and the ligamcntum nuchae of the necks of ruminating animals, both of which are composed of about two-thirds 
elastin fibres and therefore display almost completely elastic behaviour (Nachemson & Evans, 1968). Permanew 
deformation of such ligaments by traditional stretches, therefore, would be unlikely. In general, the structure of 
ligament has to be more complcx than that of tendon, becausc joint ligaments have to control forces over a larger 
number of degrees of freedom. Thus, the stretching of ligaments requires a more extensive variety of techniques.
The collagen network of skin is a complicated three-dimensional fibrous structure which allows it to deform 
considerably without necessitating elongation of individual fibres.
The S tructure and Function of Ligam ents and Tendons
Both ligaments and tendons are similar in the manner in which their structures gradually alter as they approach 
their attachment sites to bone. For instance, the transition from ligament to bone is gradual, with rows o f 
fibrocytes in the ligament transforming into groups of osteocytes, then gradually dispersing into the bone matm 
by way of an intermediate stage in which the cells resemble chondrocytes (Fung, 1981). Some authorities have 
divided the insertion region of ligament into four zones: the collagen fibres at the end of the ligament (Zone li 
intermesh with fibrocartilage (Zone 2), which gradually becomes mineralized fibrocartilage (Zone 3). The latter 
complcx finally merges with cortical bone (Zone 4). Thus, the stress concentration at the insertion of the ligamefl 
into the more rigid bone structure is decreased by the existence of these three progressively stiffer transitional 
composite materials (Fig 1.20).
Tendon differs from ligament in that only one end inserts into bone, whereas in most ligaments both ends 
attach to bone. Transition from tendon into bone is generally not quite as distinct as in ligament, and tendor 
inserts broadly into the main fibrous layer of the periosteum. Nevertheless, as in ligaments, the same type of 
gradual transition in four zones from collagen to bone may be identified (Fig 1.20). This structure, as before, 
minimizes the detrimental effects of sudden stretching or loading which would occur if there were an abnip: 
transition from muscle to collagen and then to bone.
Whereas ligaments are often closely associated with joint capsulcs, tendons occur in two basic forms: those 
with sheaths (called paratcnons) and others without sheaths. Sheaths generally surround tendons where large 
frictional forces are found and provide lubrication by means of synovial fluid produced by their synovial cells 
Thus, it may be seen that tendons with sheaths have a larger PEC than unsheathed tendons and any stretching 
the relaxed state will probably have a greater effect on the sheath. The tendon itself comprises primarily the SE C  
which is tensed only when its attendant muscle is active. This again emphasizes that different stretchinj 
techniques are necessary for enhancing the extensibility of the different tissues (see 3.5.8).

degenerative process, but also to reduced physical activity, superimposed disease states and other

Studies of the mechanical and biochemical properties of tendon reveal a close relationship between tensile strength

The tensile properties of collagenous tissues are determined by the type, structure and amount of collagen. 
There are at least ten distinct types of collagen, each with a different chain composition and occurring in various 
forms in different subsystems of the body (von dcr Mark, 1981). At a microscopic level, the characteristic 
mechanical strength of collagen depends largely on the cross-links between the collagen molecules. It has bees 
shown that the type of exercise can affect the properties of muscle, a fact which relates to these collagen cross­
links, rather than merely to the actin-myosin complcx. For example, muscle endurance training increases the 
tensile strength of both slow and fast muscles, as well as the elasticity of the former (Kovancn et al, 1984). Other 
studies have shown that prolonged running also increases the concentration of collagen in tendon and the ultimate 
tensile strength of tendon (Woo ct al, 1981). This finding is relevant to the limited prescription of off-scasoo 
transitional or general physical preparation (GPP) training.
In contrast with this finding, the concentration of collagcn in muscle is not altered by endurance training 
However, the increase in elasticity and tensile strength of the more collagenous slow musclcs after trainuij 
suggests that collagen must undergo some structural changes. In this respect, it is possible that these changes in  
the mechanical properties of slow muscles are related to stabilisation of the reducible cross-links of collagen 
(Kovancn, 1984).
With more specific reference to muscle tissue, it has been proposed that ST fibres may be able to sustais 
cross-bridge attachments for a longer period than FT fibres (Bosco et al, 1982). Therefore, the former would 
utilise the elastic energy stored in their cross-bridges more efficiently during slow movements. In addition, thii 
process may be augmented by the behaviour of the conncctive tissue in each given muscle in determining the 
ability of the slow and fast muscles to perform different types of work (Kovanen et al, 1984). Slow muscles w ith 
their greater content of strongly cross-linked collagcn would then be more adapted to slow contraction, since the 
fairly rigid collagcnous conncctive tissue would resist fast contraction. The less rigid connective tissue in fast 
muscle, on the other hand, would facilitate fast movements with greater changes in form.
The differences noted in the collagenous components of different muscle types could also imply that a slow

efficiency of slow muscle in postural and endurance tasks.

meromyosin heads of the cross-bridges and by elongation of its tail, which appears to have a helical structure that 
would promote extensibility (Huxley, 1974). In other words, even a contracted muscle can stretch, not only due 
to its collagenous component, but also due to its contractile tissue.
As stated earlier, if a relaxed muscle is stretched beyond its resting length, it is the PEC which appears to be 
most exposed to the resulting tension, whereas in active muscle it is the SEC which is subjected to most tension. 
This implies that static, relaxed ballistic and passive stretching have the greatest effect on the PEC, while tense 
ballistic and active stretching affects predominantly the SEC. The various physiotherapeutic PNF (Proprioceptive 
Neuromuscular Facilitation) flexibility techniques appear to be able to stretch and strengthen both the SEC and

the PEC, as well as the associated muscles. Weight and other rcsistancc training routines based on the same PNF 
principles can achieve similar results.
F urther Inform ation on C ollagenous Tissue
The connective tissues comprise essentially three types of fibre, namely collagen, elastin and reticulin, with the 
former two fibres constituting approximately 90% of the whole. The collagen fibres (of which there are at least 1 0  
distinct types) impart strength and stiffness to the tissue, the elastin provides compliancc or extensibility under 
loading, and reticulin furnishes bulk (Fung, 1981). The elastic fibres occur in small concentrations in the 
intercellular matrix of tendons and most ligaments, but their function is not entirely clear. It has been suggested 
that they may play a role in restoring the crimped collagen fibre configuration after stretching or musck 
contraction (Minns et al, 1973).
The behaviour of the collagenous tissues in response to mechanical stress depends on the structural 
orientation of the fibres, the properties of the collagcn and elastin fibres, and the relative proportions of collagen 
and elastin. The structural orientation of the fibres differs for the various collagenous tissues and is specifically 
suited to the functions of each tissue.
In particular, the tendon fibres are closely packed and virtually parallel, but for a slight waviness in tk 
relaxed state. This simplicity of structure suffices for tendon, since the latter usually has to transmit force} 
linearly from one point to another. In ligaments and joint capsules the fibre organisation, though still generally 
parallel, is less uniform and often oblique or spiral, its exact structure depending on the function of the particular 
ligament. Most ligaments arc purely collagenous, the only elastin fibres being those which are associated with the 
blood vessels. Virtually the only ligaments which arc mostly elastin are the ligamentum flavum of the human spine 
and the ligamcntum nuchae of the necks of ruminating animals, both of which are composed of about two-thirds 
elastin fibres and therefore display almost completely elastic behaviour (Nachemson & Evans, 1968). Permanew 
deformation of such ligaments by traditional stretches, therefore, would be unlikely. In general, the structure of 
ligament has to be more complcx than that of tendon, becausc joint ligaments have to control forces over a larger 
number of degrees of freedom. Thus, the stretching of ligaments requires a more extensive variety of techniques.
The collagen network of skin is a complicated three-dimensional fibrous structure which allows it to deform 
considerably without necessitating elongation of individual fibres.
The S tructure and Function of Ligam ents and Tendons
Both ligaments and tendons are similar in the manner in which their structures gradually alter as they approach 
their attachment sites to bone. For instance, the transition from ligament to bone is gradual, with rows o f 
fibrocytes in the ligament transforming into groups of osteocytes, then gradually dispersing into the bone matm 
by way of an intermediate stage in which the cells resemble chondrocytes (Fung, 1981). Some authorities have 
divided the insertion region of ligament into four zones: the collagen fibres at the end of the ligament (Zone li 
intermesh with fibrocartilage (Zone 2), which gradually becomes mineralized fibrocartilage (Zone 3). The latter 
complcx finally merges with cortical bone (Zone 4). Thus, the stress concentration at the insertion of the ligamefl 
into the more rigid bone structure is decreased by the existence of these three progressively stiffer transitional 
composite materials (Fig 1.20).
Tendon differs from ligament in that only one end inserts into bone, whereas in most ligaments both ends 
attach to bone. Transition from tendon into bone is generally not quite as distinct as in ligament, and tendor 
inserts broadly into the main fibrous layer of the periosteum. Nevertheless, as in ligaments, the same type of 
gradual transition in four zones from collagen to bone may be identified (Fig 1.20). This structure, as before, 
minimizes the detrimental effects of sudden stretching or loading which would occur if there were an abnip: 
transition from muscle to collagen and then to bone.
Whereas ligaments are often closely associated with joint capsulcs, tendons occur in two basic forms: those 
with sheaths (called paratcnons) and others without sheaths. Sheaths generally surround tendons where large 
frictional forces are found and provide lubrication by means of synovial fluid produced by their synovial cells 
Thus, it may be seen that tendons with sheaths have a larger PEC than unsheathed tendons and any stretching 
the relaxed state will probably have a greater effect on the sheath. The tendon itself comprises primarily the SE C  
which is tensed only when its attendant muscle is active. This again emphasizes that different stretchinj 
techniques are necessary for enhancing the extensibility of the different tissues (see 3.5.8).

However, the increase in elasticity and tensile strength of the more collagenous slow musclcs after trainuij

# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)

**What it is** — A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle; FT
fibres store more elastic energy overall. Static/relaxed/passive stretching mainly loads
the PEC; tensed/active stretching (and PNF techniques) load both the SEC and PEC. (PDF
pp. 51-52, printed pp. 40-41.)

**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's calf (fast, elastic, SEC-dominant) and a
postural trunk muscle (slower, stiffer, PEC/collagen-dominant) would, by this model, be
expected to respond differently to the same static-stretch dose, supporting muscle-specific
rather than uniform flexibility prescription.

**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

--- idx 45 (printed 34) ---
SUPERTRAINING
• The density of muscle fibres per unit cross-sectional area
• The efficiency of mechanical leverage across the joint
Functional Factors
• The number of muscle fibres contracting simultaneously
• The rate of contraction of muscle fibres
• The efficiency of synchronisation of firing of the muscle fibres
• The conduction velocity in the nerve fibres
• The degree of inhibition of muscle fibres which do not contribute to the movement
• The proportion of large diameter muscle fibres activc
• The efficiency of cooperation between different types of muscle fibre
• The efficiency of the various stretch reflexes in controlling muscic tension
• The excitation threshold of the nerve fibres supplying the musclcs
• The initial length of the muscles before contraction
With reference to the concept of synchronising action among muscle fibres and groups, it is important to point 
out that synchronisation does not appear to play a major role in increasing the rate of strength production (Miller 
et al, 1981). Efficiency of sequentiality  rather than simultaneity  may be more important in generating and 
sustaining muscular force, especially if stored elastic energy has to be contributed at the most opportune 
moments into the movement process. Certainly, more research has to be conducted before a definite answer can 
be given to the question of strength increase with increased synchronisation of motor unit discharge.
Shock Training and Plyom etrics
Although not mentioned in the preceding list, the connective tissues also play a vital structural role in the strength 
process, since they provide stability for the muscles, joints and bones, as well as the ability to store elastic energy 
for augmenting the working effect of muscle.
The ability to stretch the connective and elastic tissues increases the efficiency of human movement very 
markedly, especially as numerous sporting activities involve stretch-shortening of the muscle complex, such a$  
running, jumping, throwing and rapid lifting.
In fact, the method now known as plyometric training  and developed as a special speed-strength training 
method by Vcrkhoshansky relies entirely on this phenomenon (discussed in later chapters). In this process, the 
increase in concentric strength in response to rapid ’shock' loading is a result of increased muscle tension elicited 
by the powerful myotatic stretch reflex and  the explosive release of elastic energy stored in the connective and 
elastic tissues of the muscle complex during eccentric muscic contraction.
It must be pointed out that the term plyometric  has been applied more recently to what was originally called 
the shock method  (udamiye metod) in Russia. Historically, it was apparently coined to mean eccentric 
contraction.  In this schcmc of nomenclature, isometric  retained its original meaning of muscic contraction under 
static conditions, miometric  ('muscle shortening action’) was synonymous with concentric contraction, and 
pliometric  (sic) referred to eccentric (muscle lengthening) contraction.

aerobics') and athletics training as 'plyometrics'. Invariably, the exercises referred to as being plyometric in these

jumps' for lower limb rebound methods. If confusion with electric shock is to be avoided, then it might be 
preferable to refer to explosive reactive methods as impulsive training.  However, the persuasive appeal of 
popular usage will no doubt ensure that the term plyometrics  is retained in preference to any other word, no 
matter how inappropriate. For instance, despite the inaccuracy of the term aerobics in describing exercise to 
music and cross training  to describe supplementary sports training, the commercial market has decreed that these 
popular terms should be the definitive words to use.

accuracy. Thus, the term plyometrics  (as opposed to pliometric  contraction) should be used to refer to methods

complex and aid it in producing usable strength. Recently, it has been found that increases in the quality (or type) 
and quantity of connective tissue may improve the transmission of force from individual muscic fibres to the 
skeletal system.
For example, an insufficiently strong or extensive sheath of connective tissue will allow the muscle to dissi­
pate some of its force in a direction which is perpendicular to its line of action and thereby lower its efficiency in 
overcoming a load.

capsules, skin and cartilages play the vital role of passively stabilising the joints, facilitating contact between 
moving parts and absorbing shock. The importance of this passive role should not be forgotten in overall 
training, since it is pointless to develop bulk and strength if the remainder of the musculoskeletal system is not 
equipped to handle the increased strength. One must condition muscle, bone and connective tissue if overall per­
formance and safety is to be enhanced.

produce a muscle complex which is prone to injury and inefficient in generating reactive strength. This is one

minimising the occurrence of connective tissue soreness and injury, particularly during the general physical 
preparation phase (GPP) and by relative novices to strength training.

particularly in view of the side effects of drugs and the ethics of their use.

# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, in the original Russian nomenclature, "pliometric"
referred specifically to eccentric (lengthening) contraction, distinct from "isometric"
(static) and "miometric" (concentric, shortening); the term "plyometrics," as adopted in
the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of jumping drills, many of which do
not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. Verkhoshansky's preferred precise
definition: an eccentric contraction suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric
contraction, producing a powerful myotatic reflex and a rapid extension of the muscle's
passive components, followed by an explosive concentric contraction. (PDF p. 45, printed
p. 34.)

**Why it works** — The stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation plus
elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism; Verkhoshansky himself notes this drift and recommends "shock
method" or "depth jumps" as the more precise Russian-tradition terms (PDF p. 45, printed
p. 34). This terminology distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or
appropriate for a given athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

definition of the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, "pliometric" "was apparently coined to mean eccentric
contraction"; in this scheme of nomenclature (the text does not state it to be
specifically Russian), isometric retained its meaning of static contraction, miometric
meant concentric contraction, and pliometric meant eccentric contraction (printed 34); the
term "plyometrics," as adopted in the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of
jumping drills, many of which do not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. The
text's precise redefinition: the term plyometrics should refer to "an eccentric muscle
contraction ... suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric contraction, thereby
producing a powerful myotatic reflex, a sharp extension of the passive components of the
muscle complex and a subsequent explosive concentric contraction," and "should not refer
to ordinary jumping" (printed 34-35). (PDF pp. 45-46, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — The stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation plus
elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism; Verkhoshansky himself notes this drift and recommends "shock
method" or "depth jumps" as the more precise Russian-tradition terms (PDF p. 45, printed
p. 34). This terminology distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or
appropriate for a given athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

# The Shock Method (Original Russian "Udarnyi Metod"), and Why "Plyometrics" Is a Loose Translation

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky developed the "shock method" (udarnyi metod) as a special
speed-strength training method exploiting connective and elastic tissue's ability to
store and release elastic energy during stretch-shortening of the muscle complex (running,
jumping, throwing, rapid lifting). The rise in concentric strength after rapid "shock"
loading comes from two sources: increased muscle tension from the myotatic (stretch)
reflex, and explosive release of elastic energy stored in connective/elastic tissue during
the eccentric phase. Historically, "pliometric" "was apparently coined to mean eccentric
contraction"; in this scheme of nomenclature (the text does not state it to be
specifically Russian), isometric retained its meaning of static contraction, miometric
meant concentric contraction, and pliometric meant eccentric contraction (printed 34); the
term "plyometrics," as adopted in the West, has drifted to describe a broader category of
jumping drills, many of which do not reproduce true shock-method characteristics. The
text's precise redefinition: the term plyometrics should refer to "an eccentric muscle
contraction ... suddenly terminated in an explosive isometric contraction, thereby
producing a powerful myotatic reflex, a sharp extension of the passive components of the
muscle complex and a subsequent explosive concentric contraction," and "should not refer
to ordinary jumping" (printed 34-35). (PDF pp. 45-46, printed pp. 34-35.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation
plus elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"
exercises actually meet Verkhoshansky's precise definition (a sudden eccentric-to-isometric-
to-concentric sequence) versus being ordinary jump training relabeled; this matters for
predicting whether the intended reactive-strength adaptation is actually being trained.
This library already traces Verkhoshansky's shock-method lineage at a higher level in
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas|The
Soviet Lineage Behind Modern Sprint-Training Ideas]]; that entry credits him with "shock
method (plyometrics)" but does not cover the terminology history or mechanism given here,
so this entry adds a genuinely new angle rather than duplicating it.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not assume every drill called "plyometric" in
current commercial or popular usage (e.g. step-aerobics-style jumping) reproduces the
shock-method mechanism. "Russian scientists prefer to retain the term 'shock method' ...
and 'depth jumps'" (printed 34), while Siff separately proposes "powermetrics" for the
whole collection of jumping and rebound methods (Siff, 1998, printed 35). This terminology
distinction does not itself tell a coach which drills are safe or appropriate for a given
athlete; that is a separate training-age and readiness question.

**Example** — **Inference:** a coach programming "plyometrics" for a novice athlete should
check whether the intended exercise involves a true rapid eccentric-to-concentric shock
transition (a depth jump) or is really just a submaximal hop/jump drill; the two carry very
different neuromuscular demands despite sharing the popular label.

**Related** — [[framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional]],
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas]]
(reciprocal link recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.6 gives the
isometric/miometric/pliometric terminology scheme and the precise mechanical definition of
the shock method that this lineage table only names in passing).

# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone

**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)

**Why it works** — The reduced integrated EMG "suggest[s] that the prime movers were less
activated" during bilateral effort (printed 28). Inference: the absence of a deficit in
weightlifters, who train the bilateral pattern extensively, suggests it is trainable.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back
squat, bench, clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise
variants, match the training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports
with genuinely unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and
change-of-direction actions), this text's finding argues for meaningful unilateral training
exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts, since bilateral-only training may under-develop
the single-limb activation football and track actions require. This football-specific
application is this entry's own extension, not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts
altogether; compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are
appropriate where the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting
actions). Verkhoshansky gives no specific deficit magnitude for team-sport athletes in
this section (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28); **Inference:** the deficit's size and
trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, which is this entry's own caution.

**Example** — Inference: single-leg strength work trains the unilateral expression that
sprint and cutting actions use; bilateral 1RM alone may not show it.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]],
[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--unilateral-isometric-exposes-hidden-asymmetry]].

# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed

**What it is** — Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)

**Why it works** — Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
of 1RM.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's
velocity-based training (VBT) cueing — "move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on
submaximal sets are a modern implementation of the same idea. **Eric's baseline:** Perch
camera-based velocity-based training is part of the department's current technology stack
(`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7`). **Inference:** CAT's proprioceptive-feedback
logic maps onto that existing Perch capability, though neither the book nor the baseline
draws this connection directly. **Inference:** also useful as coaching language for
eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent) and isometric holds (actively
maintaining tension); this extension beyond the text's own concentric framing is this
entry's own reading of Verkhoshansky's eccentric/isometric CAT discussion (PDF p. 32,
printed p. 21).

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a technique/cueing concept, not a
load-prescription protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme
on its own in the text. **Inference:** cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is
not appropriate for all training goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work
deliberately avoids this); this caveat is not addressed in this section of the text.

**Example** — **Inference:** Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.

**Related** — [[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky lists the factors that determine how much strength a
muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
printed pp. 33-34.)

**Why it works** — This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
rather than assuming a training-volume problem).

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky notes more research is needed before drawing a
firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
factors alone.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
convention.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.

**Related** — [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 60-80 |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works** — Each goal loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently:
near-maximal loads at low reps bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength);
high-velocity submaximal loads bias rate of force development (power); moderate loads at
moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads
at very high reps bias oxidative/metabolic endurance.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
baseline material does not cite Verkhoshansky's specific terminology.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states this chart is "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 22, printed p.
11), and ignores the other prescription variables covered in
[[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]] and later chapters. **Inference:** do
not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

**Example** — **Inference:** Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
adjustments the text says this table omits.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].

| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 6-80 (as printed; probably a misprint for 60-80) |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with

14	# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
17	ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
18	1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
19	competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
20	and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
21	only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
22	or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
23	Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
24	isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
27	mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
28	structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
29	than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
30	reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.
31	
32	**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
33	maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
34	comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
35	**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
36	anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department
37	prefers VBT-estimated 1RM (Perch) over live 1RM attempts, estimating toward a target mean
38	velocity rather than forcing a true competitive-maximum attempt in the weight room
39	(`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`).
40	**Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's logic of anchoring
41	intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the baseline document
42	does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
45	protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which Verkhoshansky
46	himself calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
47	maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
48	(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
49	and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. Verkhoshansky states
50	the eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering is a general tendency, not a fixed ratio,
51	varying by joint angle, velocity, and muscle group (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2, cross-referenced
52	to 1.2).
53	
54	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
55	what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
56	rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
57	competitive performance.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
60	gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
61	(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).
