14	# Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things
15	
16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
17	terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
18	intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
19	that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
20	state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
21	it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
22	fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
23	"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
24	sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
25	printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
28	state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
29	objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
30	still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
31	base.
32	
33	**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical
34	capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness
35	(day-to-day fluctuation) in the department's own testing philosophy, with both tracked
36	because they answer different questions (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
37	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7`). **Inference:** that distinction maps
38	closely onto this framework's fitness/preparedness split (fitness ~ the baseline's
39	"preparedness," Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" ~ the baseline's "readiness"), though the
40	two sources use the words differently and neither cites the other; a reader moving between
41	them should track the underlying concept, not the label.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters — do not assume
44	"preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is
45	meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its
46	"preparedness." This entry's own definitions above use Verkhoshansky's terms throughout.
47	
48	**Example** — **Inference:** an athlete whose long-term strength and conditioning markers
49	(fitness/base preparedness) have been stable for weeks can still show a depressed CMJ
50	reading (Verkhoshansky's "instantaneous preparedness," the baseline's "readiness") after
51	poor sleep or travel, without any real loss of underlying capacity.
52	
53	**Related** — [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].
54

13	
14	# Deeper Knee Flexion Reduces "Shock" Loading; Fibre-Type Mix Should Guide Jump Tempo
15	
16	**What it is** — Two related findings on individualizing plyometric prescription.
17	(1) Soft-tissue spring stiffness around the knee drops sharply with flexion angle
18	(Greene & McMahon, cited PDF p. 58, printed p. 47: roughly 120 kN/m at 0 degrees down to
19	30 kN/m at 75 degrees), so the Series Elastic Component's contribution falls as knee
20	flexion increases, meaning deeper-flexion landings reduce the "shock" character of a
21	plyometric exercise. (2) Vertical jump testing found rapid, short-range stretch phases
22	were most beneficial for the vastus medialis (fast-twitch-rich), while knee extensors of
23	athletes with more slow-twitch fibres (e.g. distance runners) benefited more from slower,
24	larger-amplitude jumps with a longer transition between stretch and shortening (Bosco et
25	al., 1982), attributed to differing cross-bridge lifetimes between fibre types. (PDF pp.
26	57-58, printed pp. 46-47.)
27	
28	**Why it works** — Both findings trace back to the same underlying mechanics: SEC
29	contribution and cross-bridge dynamics vary with joint angle and fibre-type composition,
30	so a jump protocol that is optimal for one joint angle or one athlete's fibre profile is
31	not automatically optimal for another.
32	
33	**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports limiting knee flexion depth in depth-jump and
34	shock-method work specifically when the goal is maximal elastic/reactive loading (deeper
35	flexion shifts the exercise toward general strength/power rather than true "shock"
36	stimulus), and supports considering an athlete's likely fibre-type profile (position,
37	event, or direct biopsy/proxy data if available) when choosing fast-short vs.
38	slow-larger-amplitude jump variants.
39	
40	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** fibre-type composition is rarely measured directly
41	in a collegiate athletics setting; do not treat sport or position alone as a reliable proxy
42	without other supporting evidence (this entry's application to specific positions is its
43	own inference, not stated in the text). The specific stiffness values (120 kN/m to 30
44	kN/m) come from one biomechanics study on a flexible-board bouncing task, not from a
45	depth-jump or standard field-testing setup, so treat them as illustrative of the trend
46	rather than as target numbers.
47	
48	**Example** — **Inference:** a shallow-knee-flexion, low-amplitude rebound drill better
49	targets true reactive/shock adaptation than a deep-squat-style jump, which behaves more
50	like a general power exercise; a distance-oriented athlete may respond better to a slightly
51	slower, larger-amplitude jump variant than a power-position athlete.
52	
53	**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
54	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
55

13	
14	# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System
15	
16	**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
17	cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
18	system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
19	repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
20	one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
21	sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
22	wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
23	planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
24	weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
25	technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — The underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid synaptic
28	change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established. The
29	extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids will
30	measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference, not a
31	finding directly tested in athletes in this section.
32	
33	**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
34	free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
35	is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
36	across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
37	**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
38	value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
39	advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
40	(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
41	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
42	that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
43	about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
44	neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.
45	
46	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this should be treated as contested where it
47	implies routine machine use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport
48	skill; the text (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that

# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — The underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid synaptic
change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established. The
extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids will
measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference, not a
finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.

value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work

neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

implies routine machine use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport
skill; the text (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that
extension, and machines and supportive equipment remain standard tools in most strength
programs with no established injury or transfer cost at typical use levels documented
anywhere in this ingest. **Inference:** do not use this heuristic to argue against belts
for heavy compound lifts, where the safety benefit is well established elsewhere and not
addressed by this section of the text at all.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

--- idx 23 (printed 12) ---
SUPERTRAINING
Training programmes based entirely on these variables, however, are seriously incomplete and limited in their 
long-term effectiveness, especially as a form of supplementary training for other sports. Factors such as the 
following must also be taken into consideration:
• the type of strength fitness required
• the type of muscle contraction involved (isometric, concentric, eccentric)
• the speed of movement over different phases of movement
• the acceleration at critical points in the movement
• the rest intervals between repetitions, sets and workouts
• active versus passive rest/recuperation intervals
• the sequence of exercises
• the relative strength of agonists and antagonists, stabilisers and movers
• the development of optimal static and dynamic range of movement
• the strength deficit of given muscle groups
• the training history of the individual
• the injury history of the individual
• the level of sports proficiency of the individual.
The last-mentioned factor is of exceptional importance, because the advanced athlete responds to a given training 
regime very differently from a novice. For instance, the exact sequencing of strength, strcngth-speed and 
hypertrophy means in a workout or microcycle is of little consequence during the first weeks or months of a 
beginner's training, but is very important to a more experienced athlete. Moreover, loads as small as 40% of 1RM 
can significantly enhance the strength of a beginner, but have no strengthening effect on an elite athlete.
1.1.2 Factors Lim iting Strength Production
The production of strength in the short and long term depends on the following main factors:
• Trainability • Pain and Fear of Pain
• Neuromuscular Efficiency • Injury and Fear of Injury
• Biomechanical Efficiency • Fatigue
• Psychological Factors
Trainability This refers to the potential to develop strength in response to a specific training regime and 
depends largely on genetic factors and pre-training status. Genetic factors determine the potential for 
hypertrophy, the leverage characteristics about each joint, the distribution of fast and slow twitch fibres in the 
different muscle groups, and metabolic efficiency. The pre-training status refers to the level of special fitness 
possessed by an individual before formal training begins. Physical loading imposed by work, play and casual 
sport has a pronounced effect on one's ability to gain strength, with the greatest relative increases being possible 
among untrained individuals and the smallest among elite athletes. Individual response to training at a given level 
of special fitness, however, is governed largely by one’s genetic predisposition to increase hypertrophy, strength 
and power easily. Moreover, during long-term training, the blood serum levels of biologically active unbound 
testosterone may also be of importance for trainability (Hakkinen, 1985).
Neuromuscular Efficiency This refers to the skill with which one executes a given movement and relates to how 
efficiently and intensively one recruits muscle fibres in the appropriate muscle groups to produce the movement 
pattern accurately and powerfully. All motor action is controlled by nervous and neuromuscular processes, so 
that this factor should be regarded as fundamental to the functional production of strength.
Biomechanical Efficiency This relates to genetic factors such as the leverage characteristics of the body, the 
relative strengths of the different muscle groups controlling the movement of each limb, and the neuromuscular 
efficiency which orchestrates all movement patterns of the body. The efficiency of movements with and without 
the use of sporting apparel and equipment (such as bats, racquets and throwing implements) or in close contact 
with opponents (e.g. in wrestling, judo, rugby and American football) is especially important. Unlike the 
immutable genetic factors which predispose one person to achieve a potential which far exceeds that of another 
person, both neuromuscular and biomechanical efficiency are profoundly influenced by training and offer a vehicle 
for producing great increases in strength, as will be seen in later chapters.
12

# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
(active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
the novice.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
risk rather than Verkhoshansky's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; Verkhoshansky's text does not
draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.

**Example** — **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related** — [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].

# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — The underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid synaptic
change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established. The
extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids will
measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference, not a
finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this should be treated as contested where it
implies routine machine use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport
skill; the text (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that
extension, and machines and supportive equipment remain standard tools in most strength
programs with no established injury or transfer cost at typical use levels documented
anywhere in this ingest. **Inference:** do not use this heuristic to argue against belts
for heavy compound lifts, where the safety benefit is well established elsewhere and not
addressed by this section of the text at all.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].

element has not been associated with the PEC, because there is minimal movement between structures such as the 
saroolemma and sheaths around the muscle fibres which are considered to comprise the PEC.

# Deeper Knee Flexion Reduces "Shock" Loading; Fibre-Type Mix Should Guide Jump Tempo

**What it is** — Two related findings on individualizing plyometric prescription.
(1) Soft-tissue spring stiffness around the knee drops sharply with flexion angle
(Greene & McMahon, cited PDF p. 58, printed p. 47: roughly 120 kN/m at 0 degrees down to
30 kN/m at 75 degrees), so the Series Elastic Component's contribution falls as knee
flexion increases, meaning deeper-flexion landings reduce the "shock" character of a
plyometric exercise. (2) Vertical jump testing found rapid, short-range stretch phases
were most beneficial for the vastus medialis (fast-twitch-rich), while knee extensors of
athletes with more slow-twitch fibres (e.g. distance runners) benefited more from slower,
larger-amplitude jumps with a longer transition between stretch and shortening (Bosco et
al., 1982), attributed to differing cross-bridge lifetimes between fibre types. (PDF pp.
57-58, printed pp. 46-47.)

**Why it works** — Both findings trace back to the same underlying mechanics: SEC
contribution and cross-bridge dynamics vary with joint angle and fibre-type composition,
so a jump protocol that is optimal for one joint angle or one athlete's fibre profile is
not automatically optimal for another.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports limiting knee flexion depth in depth-jump and
shock-method work specifically when the goal is maximal elastic/reactive loading (deeper
flexion shifts the exercise toward general strength/power rather than true "shock"
stimulus), and supports considering an athlete's likely fibre-type profile (position,
event, or direct biopsy/proxy data if available) when choosing fast-short vs.
slow-larger-amplitude jump variants.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** fibre-type composition is rarely measured directly
in a collegiate athletics setting; do not treat sport or position alone as a reliable proxy
without other supporting evidence (this entry's application to specific positions is its
own inference, not stated in the text). The specific stiffness values (120 kN/m to 30
kN/m) come from one biomechanics study on a flexible-board bouncing task, not from a
depth-jump or standard field-testing setup, so treat them as illustrative of the trend
rather than as target numbers.

**Example** — **Inference:** a shallow-knee-flexion, low-amplitude rebound drill better
targets true reactive/shock adaptation than a deep-squat-style jump, which behaves more
like a general power exercise; a distance-oriented athlete may respond better to a slightly
slower, larger-amplitude jump variant than a power-position athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** the department

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) separates "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — Verkhoshansky states the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`; flagged there as
"Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol)," and that same Assessment Manual is
separately flagged as likely outdated since it is built around GymAware, not the current

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength, flexibility-endurance,
flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill, speed-skill, and
skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass) matter
separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF pp.
102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works** — Rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and flexibility as
four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise and triple
combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually appear in
sport (e.g. "speed-strength" and "strength-speed" as two distinct qualities depending on
which end of the force-velocity spectrum dominates, already discussed in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]), with skill/
neuromuscular control cutting across all of them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
speed-strength endurance, strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength,
flexibility-endurance, flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill,
speed-skill, and skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass)
matter separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF
pp. 102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works** — Inference: rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and
flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
speed-strength split already used in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. distinguishing
"strength-speed" training from "speed-strength" training, or "flexibility-strength" from
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific,
combinable qualities.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 102, printed p. 91);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example** — **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again

**What it is** — Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)

**Why it works** — This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky himself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.

**Example** — **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.

**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

16	**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
17	voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
18	ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
19	difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
20	absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
21	action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
22	risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
23	a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
24	sudden dip (printed 9).
25	
26	The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
27	and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
28	is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
29	nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
30	the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
31	using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
32	9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
33	if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
34	may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
35	weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
36	induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
37	conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
38	the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
39	5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
40	work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
41	20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
42	credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)
43	
44	The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
45	difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
46	training algorithm" (`research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-
47	countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`), which independently argues against

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
training algorithm" (`research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-
countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`), which independently argues against
using either of this book's two directions as a programming rule.

**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: SJ-vs-CMJ comparison on ForceDecks is a
modern, instrumented analogue of this book's proposed proxy, but given the book's internal
conflict and Kozinc et al. (2022)'s finding that the difference does not validate a
training algorithm, this entry gives no basis for deriving a training-emphasis rule from
that comparison.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this framework to set training emphasis from an
SJ/CMJ-style gap in either direction; the book contradicts itself on which direction is
which (printed 9-10), and the modern evidence on this specific test (Kozinc et al. 2022)
does not support a diagnostic cutoff or algorithm built on it. Use RSI, mRSI, or other
modern jump-testing metrics on their own validated basis instead of this 1990s-era
heuristic.

**Example** — Inference: no training-emphasis direction can be taken from this source; see
Kozinc et al. (2022) for the modern evidence on SJ-CMJ differences.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]],
[[research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip]].

21	> **Citation**
22	> Kozinc Ž, Žitnik J, Smajla D, Šarabon N. The difference between squat jump and countermovement jump in 770 male and female participants from different sports. *European Journal of Sport Science*. 2022;22(7):985-993. doi:10.1080/17461391.2021.1936654.
23	
24	## Why it was promoted
25	
26	This study directly challenges the common assumption that a larger countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference is inherently desirable. It provides a large multisport dataset and a practical caution against treating a composite jump-difference score as a standalone marker of stretch-shortening-cycle quality or training need.
27	
28	## Research question
29	
30	Do athlete groups with better squat-jump and countermovement-jump performance also show a larger relative difference between those jumps, and how do sport and sex relate to the three outcomes?
31	
32	## Population and context
33	
34	The convenience sample included 712 competitive athletes and 58 physically active physical-education students across basketball, dance, karate, long-distance running, soccer, speed skating, tennis, short-distance running, and volleyball. Mean subgroup ages ranged from 15.7 to 36.3 years; soccer and volleyball included only males, and subgroup sizes were highly unequal. [p. 3]
35	
36	## Study design and methods
37	
38	This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion. Jump height was derived from force-platform impulse and takeoff velocity; the best trial was retained, and the relative difference was calculated as (CMJ minus SJ) divided by SJ times 100. Two-way ANOVA examined sport and sex effects, with correlations used for secondary associations. [p. 4]
39	
40	## Key findings
41	
42	- Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. [p. 5]
43	- Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. [p. 5]
44	- Physical-education students showed the largest relative jump difference despite not being the highest-performing jump group, whereas most athlete groups had broadly similar values. [p. 6]
45	- The relative difference was moderately associated with countermovement-jump height across the full sample (r = 0.41) but was not associated with squat-jump height (r = 0.03); this association does not identify the mechanism producing the difference. [p. 6]
46	- Sport-group patterns differed depending on whether the outcome was jump height, peak power, or push-off time, undermining a single universal interpretation of the countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference. [p. 7]
47	- The authors concluded that a larger difference is not necessarily better and may reflect several factors, including muscle-tendon slack, rate-of-force-development capability, technique, or task familiarity rather than only superior stretch-shortening-cycle use. [p. 9]
48	
49	## Limitations and applicability
50	
51	The cross-sectional design cannot establish why groups differed or how training changes the metric. Recruitment was by convenience; subgroup ages, sizes, sex representation, and training backgrounds were unbalanced, with very small speed-skating and sprint subgroups and no women in soccer or volleyball. Within-group variability was substantial, the best trial rather than an average was analyzed, and the composite difference inherits error from both jump tests. [p. 8] No collegiate American football players were studied, so direct norm transfer is inappropriate. The broad measurement lesson is applicable, but football-specific reference values and longitudinal sensitivity require local validation.
52	
53	## Practitioner interpretation
54	
55	Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone. Examine the two component jumps, their force-time characteristics, technique quality, reliability, and change relative to the athlete’s own typical error. In collegiate American football, use position- and athlete-specific longitudinal baselines and pair any difference score with direct measures relevant to the question, such as jump height, impulse, strategy, or force-velocity characteristics. This paper supports cautious interpretation; it does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a training algorithm.

# Kozinc et al. 2022 — Squat-jump and countermovement-jump difference across sports

> **Citation**
> Kozinc Ž, Žitnik J, Smajla D, Šarabon N. The difference between squat jump and countermovement jump in 770 male and female participants from different sports. *European Journal of Sport Science*. 2022;22(7):985-993. doi:10.1080/17461391.2021.1936654.

## Why it was promoted

This study directly challenges the common assumption that a larger countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference is inherently desirable. It provides a large multisport dataset and a practical caution against treating a composite jump-difference score as a standalone marker of stretch-shortening-cycle quality or training need.

## Research question

Do athlete groups with better squat-jump and countermovement-jump performance also show a larger relative difference between those jumps, and how do sport and sex relate to the three outcomes?

## Population and context

The convenience sample included 712 competitive athletes and 58 physically active physical-education students across basketball, dance, karate, long-distance running, soccer, speed skating, tennis, short-distance running, and volleyball. Mean subgroup ages ranged from 15.7 to 36.3 years; soccer and volleyball included only males, and subgroup sizes were highly unequal. [p. 3]

## Study design and methods

This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion. Jump height was derived from force-platform impulse and takeoff velocity; the best trial was retained, and the relative difference was calculated as (CMJ minus SJ) divided by SJ times 100. Two-way ANOVA examined sport and sex effects, with correlations used for secondary associations. [p. 4]

## Key findings

- Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. [p. 5]
- Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. [p. 5]
- Physical-education students showed the largest relative jump difference despite not being the highest-performing jump group, whereas most athlete groups had broadly similar values. [p. 6]
- The relative difference was moderately associated with countermovement-jump height across the full sample (r = 0.41) but was not associated with squat-jump height (r = 0.03); this association does not identify the mechanism producing the difference. [p. 6]
- Sport-group patterns differed depending on whether the outcome was jump height, peak power, or push-off time, undermining a single universal interpretation of the countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference. [p. 7]
- The authors concluded that a larger difference is not necessarily better and may reflect several factors, including muscle-tendon slack, rate-of-force-development capability, technique, or task familiarity rather than only superior stretch-shortening-cycle use. [p. 9]

## Limitations and applicability

The cross-sectional design cannot establish why groups differed or how training changes the metric. Recruitment was by convenience; subgroup ages, sizes, sex representation, and training backgrounds were unbalanced, with very small speed-skating and sprint subgroups and no women in soccer or volleyball. Within-group variability was substantial, the best trial rather than an average was analyzed, and the composite difference inherits error from both jump tests. [p. 8] No collegiate American football players were studied, so direct norm transfer is inappropriate. The broad measurement lesson is applicable, but football-specific reference values and longitudinal sensitivity require local validation.

## Practitioner interpretation

Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone. Examine the two component jumps, their force-time characteristics, technique quality, reliability, and change relative to the athlete’s own typical error. In collegiate American football, use position- and athlete-specific longitudinal baselines and pair any difference score with direct measures relevant to the question, such as jump height, impulse, strategy, or force-velocity characteristics. This paper supports cautious interpretation; it does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a training algorithm.
