=== claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.

**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in

=== claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity.md ===
**Why it works** — The reduced integrated EMG "suggest[s] that the prime movers were less
activated" during bilateral effort (printed 28). Inference: the absence of a deficit in
weightlifters, who train the bilateral pattern extensively, suggests it is trainable.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back

=== claim--collagen-loading-curve-and-injury-risk.md ===
**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static

=== claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals.md ===
**Why it works** — The author gives one mechanism: fast-twitch fibres can start behaving
like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity work (printed 59). Inference:
continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch
characteristics, a different and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the
high-force, high-velocity, largely fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's
rest intervals let each work bout stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific
zone instead of drifting toward an endurance stimulus.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming

=== claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates.md ===
**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism beyond the differing rates. Inference:
collagen turnover and remodeling are slower than muscle protein synthesis and neural
adaptation, so a program that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace
what tendon, ligament, and bone can structurally tolerate.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load

=== claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table.md ===
**Why it works** — The authors state these figures "reflect the average contributions made
by three concurrently operating metabolic systems ... for an average athlete," which
"disguises the fact ... that the metabolic demands often differ from instant to instant
during every type of activity taking place in each sport" (printed 81). Inference: for
football specifically, actual play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays)
separated by long rest (huddles, substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real
repeated-sprint, phosphagen-dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role
of aerobic recovery between bursts; the text does not itself apply this reasoning to
football.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for

=== claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force.md ===
**Why it works** — Force magnitude alone does not determine which fibres are recruited or
how force is produced; movement pattern, contact duration, and whether elastic energy
storage/release is involved (SSC-mediated ballistic actions vs. purely contractile,
non-ballistic actions) change both the recruitment pattern and the resulting force-time and
force-velocity relationships.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces

=== claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states

=== claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths.md ===
**Why it works** — Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and

=== claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table.md ===
**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material — early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
specialization later draws on. The text does not itself restate this mechanism in this
passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25). The text does note one exception: "many Russian
experts" hold that early specialization is possible in sports emphasizing coordination,
agility, flexibility, or speed (e.g. gymnastics), because of the pre-adolescent's
particular ability in those respects; strength and endurance sports are discouraged for
youngsters specifically (printed 25).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a more granular, sport-by-sport reference

=== claim--strength-training-threshold-stimulus.md ===
**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: early neuromuscular
adaptation (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]) responds to almost
any sufficiently repeated stimulus above a low floor; once that easy adaptive window
closes, further progress requires a stimulus that approaches the athlete's current
ceiling, because there is less slack left in recruitment and coordination to exploit.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports keeping early-phase (novice) load prescription

=== claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer.md ===
**Why it works** — The authors give no reason for the asymmetry itself. What they do say
(printed 29): because force decreases with velocity on the concentric F-V curve, "high
velocity training may not produce a large enough force to stimulate maximal adaptation in
the muscle," but its "special advantage ... is that it conditions the nervous system,
whereas lower velocity training is better suited to development of muscle hypertrophy and
slow speed strength." Inference: force-velocity curve position (see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]) and contraction-mode
recruitment patterns are trained narrowly because different neural drive strategies and
structural adaptations underlie each.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** when selecting exercise velocity and contraction mode,

=== claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes.md ===
**Why it works** — The authors give the protective-governor idea: "specific neural feedback
mechanisms, like governors in a mechanical engine, exist to prevent a muscle from
continuing to produce force to the point of mechanical failure" (printed 1). Inference:
both figures reflect that inhibition; anything that reduces it (competitive arousal,
hypnosis, involuntary reflex recruitment) exposes more of the muscle's true contractile
ceiling. Training may narrow the untapped reserve because part of the strength-training
adaptation is learning to recruit and inhibit less, not just growing tissue; the text does
not state this training mechanism directly.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is best used as a coaching narrative for why

=== framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms.md ===
**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

**When to apply** — The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,

=== framework--compensatory-acceleration-training.md ===
**Why it works** — Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
of 1RM.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's

=== framework--determinants-of-strength-structural-functional.md ===
**Why it works** — This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than

=== framework--factors-limiting-strength-production.md ===
**Why it works** — Strength testing and training programs typically control for load,
volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.
Reflex inhibition around an injured joint is stated in the text as "a well-known phenomenon
which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged" (Stokes & Young, 1984; printed 14).
Inference: this is not just a "mental" factor layered on top of a physical ceiling, but a
measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a checklist when an athlete's force output

=== framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing.md ===
**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning

=== framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training.md ===
**Why it works** — The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply** — The authors state functional stages should precede structural

=== framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization.md ===
**Why it works** — Because motor planning measurably begins before the muscles act,
rehearsing a movement mentally (with vivid sensory and emotional detail) engages some of
the same preparatory neural circuitry as physically performing it, giving visualization a
plausible mechanism beyond simple relaxation or confidence-building.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** supports including structured visualization/mental

=== framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology.md ===
**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic

=== framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal.md ===
**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the table itself. Inference: each goal
loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently: near-maximal loads at low reps
bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength); high-velocity submaximal loads bias
rate of force development (power); moderate loads at moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic
and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads at very high reps bias oxidative/
metabolic endurance.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a

=== framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and
flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
speed-strength split already used in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely

=== framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy.md ===
**Why it works** — The two hypertrophy types build different cellular components (more
contractile machinery per fibre vs. more non-contractile fluid/protein volume around
existing machinery), so they produce different ratios of size gain to strength gain
depending on the loading style that stimulated them.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant to explaining why an athlete can add

=== framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components.md ===
**Why it works** — Distinguishing which structure (PEC vs. SEC) is under tension during a
given stretch or contraction condition explains why different stretching methods (static
passive vs. active/PNF) target different tissue, and why fast, elastic-energy-storing
tissue (SEC-dominant, FT-rich muscle) behaves differently under rapid loading than slow,
postural (ST-rich, PEC/collagen-dominant) muscle.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength

=== framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: the stretch-shortening cycle mechanism (reflex potentiation
plus elastic energy return) is well established in modern SSC/plyometric research
independent of this text; this entry's contribution is the terminology history and the
precise mechanical definition, which distinguishes genuine shock-method work from
ordinary jumping drills marketed under the same name.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** useful when auditing whether a program's "plyometric"

=== framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks

=== framework--types-of-maximal-strength.md ===
**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply** — The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training

=== framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness.md ===
**Why it works** — Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
base.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical

=== heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type.md ===
**Why it works** — Both findings trace back to the same underlying mechanics: SEC
contribution and cross-bridge dynamics vary with joint angle and fibre-type composition,
so a jump protocol that is optimal for one joint angle or one athlete's fibre profile is
not automatically optimal for another.

**When to apply** — The text itself draws the joint-angle application: "this has profound

=== heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: the underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid
synaptic change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established.
The extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids
will measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference,
not a finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring

=== heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age.md ===
**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
the novice.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is

=== heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: a large deficit means there is untapped voluntary/neural
capacity still available, so training that improves recruitment and rate of activation (max
effort or reactive/plyometric methods) has the most room to produce gains. A small deficit
means the athlete is already recruiting close to their ceiling voluntarily, so further
gains require growing the tissue itself (hypertrophy) before neural methods can express
more force. This reasoning applies only to the "In general" rule; the source's own
jump-paragraph rule reverses it (see above).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** as a screening question for method selection, applied

=== principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods.md ===
**Why it works** — The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are
mechanically equal on that one variable but different on several others that matter
physiologically.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises

=== principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity.md ===
**Why it works** — The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of

=== principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: force output can rise before cross-sectional area change
translates into more strength through improved recruitment, firing rate, and coordination
of the muscle already present. Early strength gains outpacing measurable hypertrophy is a
replicated finding in resistance training research outside this text; whether hypertrophy
itself contributes meaningfully to early strength gains, versus being purely downstream, is
an active debate (Loenneke et al. 2019 vs. Taber et al. 2019, both Sports Med), which is
why this entry is capped at `supported` rather than `proven` for the broader "not muscle
size" framing.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this principle explains early-training-block strength

=== principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter.md ===
**Why it works** — Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is well
established in modern force-time curve analysis outside this text, which the text itself
does not cite.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the

=== principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy.md ===
**Why it works** — The cross-bridge attachment window is a hard physiological time
constraint; the mechanics of elastic energy return depend on catching that window, which
is why a fast stretch-to-shorten transition (a short "amortization phase," in later
plyometrics terminology) is functionally different from a slow, paused transition even if
the stretch magnitude is identical.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the underlying mechanism behind coaching cues

=== principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions.md ===
**Why it works** — Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. Inference: specificity itself is one of the more broadly replicated findings in
strength and conditioning research independent of this text, though the book's own
ten-dimension taxonomy and the "little or no improvement on the others" claim are the
authors' own framework, not independently established as stated.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an

=== principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique.md ===
**Why it works** — Torque = force x moment arm; for a fixed external force (a given
weight), shortening the moment arm directly lowers the rotational demand on the joint,
which is standard, independently-established biomechanics, not specific to this text.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a coaching cue and technical-fault-diagnosis

=== principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action.md ===
**Why it works** — This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
